<title>How the construction, desecration and destruction of Jerusalem’s ancient temples shaped Judaism – and Hanukkah</title>

Menorahs with seven branches, like this one in Berlin&#39;s Rykestrasse Synagogue, are meant to resemble the one in the ancient Temple.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/october-2021-berlin-a-hanukkah-chandelier-photographed-at-news-photo/1236153448?phrase=hanukkah%20temple&amp;adppopup=true">XAMAX/picture alliance via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In 167 B.C.E., on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem. According to tradition, he converted the sanctuary to a temple to Zeus. More broadly, Antiochos <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3267943">outlawed Jewish customs</a>, including <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=2%20Maccabees%207&amp;version=RSV">dietary laws</a>, circumcision and observing the Sabbath. </p>

<p>The name Epiphanes meant “manifest,” implying the king was a god on Earth, but Jewish sources <a href="https://www.bartehrman.com/antiochus-epiphanes/">called him “Epimanes”: madman</a>.</p>

<p>Three years later, on the same day of the same month, Jews in Jerusalem <a href="https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/maccabean-revolt/">scored a major victory against the Greeks</a>, and the Temple was converted back to a Jewish place of worship. Rabbinic texts written much later described how one day’s worth of oil, all that was left to rededicate the Temple, lasted for eight – <a href="https://thetorah.com/article/uncovering-the-truth-about-chanukah">the seeming miracle at the heart of the Hanukkah story</a>. </p>

<p>The holiday’s name means “dedication,” highlighting the temple’s importance for Jewish cultures. This temple, in fact, was the second version, after the first place of worship to the Jewish deity <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/topics/destruction-of-the-first-temple?sort=Relevance&amp;tab=sources">was destroyed in 586 B.C.E.</a>.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.colorado.edu/rlst/samuel-boyd">a scholar of the Bible</a> and religions drawn from it, I am fascinated by the history of the two temples in Jerusalem, which are vital for understanding the background of Hanukkah. </p>

<h2>The First Temple</h2>

<p>In ancient West Asia, temples played a pivotal role in religion, politics, the economy and even family life. In many ways, for example, they functioned like <a href="https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/f18f716f-38a5-435b-995d-0a03b35b5433">modern banks</a>, where taxes would be collected and storehouses of treasuries accumulated.  </p>

<p>Temples also served as the house of the god or goddess worshipped there. At <a href="https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/news/special-report-current-status-tell-ain-dara-temple/">a temple at Ain Dara</a>, in modern-day Syria, carvings of 10-foot-long (3-meter-long) footsteps represent a deity entering its abode. Several times, the Bible refers to the temple in Jerusalem <a href="https://biblehub.com/jps/1_kings/6.htm">as the “house of the LORD</a>.” </p>

<p>The first major temple in Jerusalem is traditionally thought to have been <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Temple-of-Jerusalem">built by King Solomon</a> in the 10th century B.C.E. Nothing of Solomon’s temple remains, but the Bible’s <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings.6.3?lang=bi&amp;with=all&amp;lang2=en">Book of 1 Kings</a> describes three main sections: an outer portico, a main hall and the “holy of holies,” an inner sanctuary.</p>

<p>The ancient Israelites’ belief that God resided in that sanctuary was foundational to the often-bewildering <a href="https://www.mohrsiebeck.com/en/book/the-story-of-sacrifice-9783161596360/">sets of rituals</a> performed at the Temple. These laws, laid out in the biblical <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus?tab=contents">Book of Leviticus</a>, were designed to keep the divine abode ritually pure. </p>

<p>After all, if the most powerful being ever lived in the Temple, keeping it clean, and keeping God happy there, would be of paramount importance. When the divine presence settled in the Temple, biblical authors claimed, <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms.46.7?lang=bi">Jerusalem could not be destroyed</a>. </p>

<p>After Solomon’s reign, ancient Israel split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south, where Jerusalem lay. Assyrians, whose large empire lay to the east, <a href="https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/article/israelites-in-exile/">conquered the north</a> in the eighth century B.C.E., and before long, their armies <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/military-history-and-science/sennacherib-invades-syro-palestine/">tried to invade Jerusalem</a>, too. They failed, fueling biblical writers’ conviction that <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Isaiah.31.4?lang=bi">Jerusalem was inviolable</a> so long as God lived there. </p>

<p>But over the years, the Bible <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Jeremiah%207&amp;version=NIV">describes religious observance in Judah growing lax</a>. As the <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezekiel%208-11&amp;version=NIV">Book of Ezekiel</a> tells it, <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ezekiel%208-11&amp;version=NIV">God departed his dwelling</a>, leaving it open to <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/nebuchadnezzar-takes-jerusalem-babylonian-captivity-begins/">destruction by the Babylonians</a> in 586 B.C.E. </p>

<h2>The Second Temple</h2>

<p>In the ancient world, many cultures believed that when a temple was destroyed, the god who dwelt there lost a battle. The victors tended to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1515/janeh-2015-0006">cart away images of the conquered cultures’ deities</a>, an act called “god-napping.” Some of those divinities <a href="https://www.eerdmans.com/9780802839725/the-early-history-of-god/">would be absorbed</a> <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/20064540">into the conquering culture’s traditions</a>. </p>

<p>After Judah’s defeat, its people were <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Babylonian-Captivity">exiled to Babylon</a>, where Iraq and Syria are today. Yet the exiled Judeans’ traditions did not disappear. Instead, they found ways to innovate. In place of the Temple and the sacrifices made there, they built <a href="https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300106282/the-ancient-synagogue/">houses of worship called “synagogues”</a> and developed new services and prayers. </p>

<p>About 50 years later, however, the Judeans received a second chance to create a divine dwelling in Jerusalem. Cyrus, king of Persia, <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/jews-return-babylonian-captivity/">decreed that they could return</a> and build a second temple. </p>

<p>When this new structure was <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Temple-of-Jerusalem">erected around 520 B.C.E.</a>, it proved initially disappointing. According to <a href="https://www.sefaria.org/Ezra.3.13?lang=bi">the Bible’s Book of Ezra</a>, those who had seen the First Temple wept for sorrow since the second was <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/759160322">a pale reflection of the first</a>.</p>

<p>Not that this was the only temple: There is archaeological evidence of <a href="https://doi.org/10.5325/b.20269759">one in Egypt</a> in the fifth century B.C.E.; and another, even earlier, in <a href="https://www.telmoza.org/">Tel Motza</a>, just a few miles from Solomon’s Temple. Scholars debate how temples were perceived in ancient Judah, since the Bible’s Book of Deuteronomy suggests that <a href="https://thetorah.com/article/how-the-jerusalem-temple-was-chosen-as-the-only-place-of-worship">only the one temple in Jerusalem should exist</a>.</p>

<p>Despite the evidence for these other temples, surviving Jewish tradition has only emphasized these two – the First and Second – in Jerusalem. </p>

<h2>Expansion – and destruction</h2>

<p>It was the Second Temple that became the object of Antiochus’ persecution – a persecution that, according to some scholars, was the <a href="https://doi.org/10.2307/3267943">first religiously motivated</a> one in history. Prior empires in the region cared little for local religious observances, as long as subjects paid taxes to the central authorities. </p>

<p>One motivation behind Antiochus’ actions may have been economic: His empire was losing ground, and fast, <a href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/116181/jerusalem-by-simon-sebag-montefiore/">in an expensive struggle</a> <a href="https://www.thecollector.com/battle-magnesia-rome-vs-seleucids/">against the Romans</a>, whose power in the Mediterranean was quickly growing. Jewish communities <a href="https://doi.org/10.1163/9789004409859_003">paid a tax to the Temple in Jerusalem</a>, so robbing its treasures may have been an attempt to replenish the empire’s depleted finances. </p>

<p>Ultimately the Jewish community in Jerusalem won out against Antiochus’ persecution. Over a century later, under King Herod, <a href="https://history.vcu.edu/news/newsroom/history-news/uncovering-herodian-archaeology-the-temple-mount-and-the-holy-city.html">the Second Temple was expanded</a> to become quite a marvel. Even Roman sources <a href="https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Cassius_Dio/37*.html">described it as a splendid edifice</a>. His reconstruction project would continue long after his life, into the early 60s C.E. </p>

<p>Only a few years later, in 70, the Romans <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/anthropology/roman-destruction-temple-jerusalem/">destroyed the Second Temple</a>. The Western Wall of the compound survives today as a testimony to Herod’s expansive construction project. </p>

<h2>Judaism without a temple</h2>

<p>Today, the place where the First and Second Temples once stood is called the Temple Mount. There has not been a third temple, <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/8/26/israeli-minister-ben-gvir-says-he-would-build-synagogue-on-al-aqsa-compound">despite some groups’</a> <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/4/9/what-do-texan-red-heifers-have-to-do-with-al-aqsa-and-a-jewish-temple">calls to build one</a>. </p>

<p>Though Jews no longer perform temple rites, studying those laws is a major focus of <a href="https://www.pennpress.org/9780812207460/the-memory-of-the-temple-and-the-making-of-the-rabbis/">the Talmud</a>, a collection of rabbinic rulings and debates. And as Hanukkah demonstrates, Jewish communities celebrate the temples through liturgy, literature and ritual. As Jews around the world light their menorahs, the holiday is a reminder of the Temple’s importance, even if it no longer exists.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297050/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: Today's Hanukkah menorahs have nine branches
body: Today's Hanukkah menorahs have nine branches
Menorahs with seven branches, like this one in Berlin's Rykestrasse Synagogue, are meant to resemble the one in the ancient Temple
XAMAX/picture alliance via Getty Images In 167 B.C.E., on the 25th day of the Hebrew month of Kislev, the Greek king Antiochos IV Epiphanes entered the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem
According to tradition, he converted the sanctuary to a temple to Zeus
More broadly, Antiochos outlawed Jewish customs , including dietary laws , circumcision and observing the Sabbath
The name Epiphanes meant “manifest,” implying the king was a god on Earth, but Jewish sources called him “Epimanes”: madman
Three years later, on the same day of the same month, Jews in Jerusalem scored a major victory against the Greeks , and the Temple was converted back to a Jewish place of worship
Rabbinic texts written much later described how one day’s worth of oil, all that was left to rededicate the Temple, lasted for eight – the seeming miracle at the heart of the Hanukkah story
The holiday’s name means “dedication,” highlighting the temple’s importance for Jewish cultures
This temple, in fact, was the second version, after the first place of worship to the Jewish deity was destroyed in 586 B.C.E.
As a scholar of the Bible and religions drawn from it, I am fascinated by the history of the two temples in Jerusalem, which are vital for understanding the background of Hanukkah
Students light candles on a Hanukkah menorah in Bnei Brak, Israel, on Dec. 28, 2016
Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images The First Temple In ancient West Asia, temples played a pivotal role in religion, politics, the economy and even family life
In many ways, for example, they functioned like modern banks , where taxes would be collected and storehouses of treasuries accumulated
Temples also served as the house of the god or goddess worshipped there
At a temple at Ain Dara , in modern-day Syria, carvings of 10-foot-long (3-meter-long) footsteps represent a deity entering its abode

Several times, the Bible refers to the temple in Jerusalem as the “house of the LORD .” The first major temple in Jerusalem is traditionally thought to have been built by King Solomon in the 10th century B.C.E
Nothing of Solomon’s temple remains, but the Bible’s Book of 1 Kings describes three main sections: an outer portico, a main hall and the “holy of holies,” an inner sanctuary
A mural from the third century C.E., found in the Dura Europos Synagogue in modern-day Syria, depicts Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem
Wikimedia Commons The ancient Israelites’ belief that God resided in that sanctuary was foundational to the often-bewildering sets of rituals performed at the Temple
These laws, laid out in the biblical Book of Leviticus , were designed to keep the divine abode ritually pure
After all, if the most powerful being ever lived in the Temple, keeping it clean, and keeping God happy there, would be of paramount importance
When the divine presence settled in the Temple, biblical authors claimed, Jerusalem could not be destroyed
After Solomon’s reign, ancient Israel split into two kingdoms: Israel in the north, and Judah in the south, where Jerusalem lay
Assyrians, whose large empire lay to the east, conquered the north in the eighth century B.C.E., and before long, their armies tried to invade Jerusalem , too
They failed, fueling biblical writers’ conviction that Jerusalem was inviolable so long as God lived there
But over the years, the Bible describes religious observance in Judah growing lax
As the Book of Ezekiel tells it, God departed his dwelling , leaving it open to destruction by the Babylonians in 586 B.C.E
An early 20th-century painting by James Tissot imagines the Babylonian’s destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.E., and exiles fleeing the city
Phillip Medhurst/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA The Second Temple In the ancient world, many cultures believed that when a temple was destroyed, the god who dwelt there lost a battle
The victors tended to cart away images of the conquered cultures’ deities , an act called “god-napping.” Some of those divinities would be absorbed into the conquering culture’s traditions
After Judah’s defeat, its people were exiled to Babylon , where Iraq and Syria are today
Yet the exiled Judeans’ traditions did not disappear
In place of the Temple and the sacrifices made there, they built houses of worship called “synagogues” and developed new services and prayers
About 50 years later, however, the Judeans received a second chance to create a divine dwelling in Jerusalem
Cyrus, king of Persia, decreed that they could return and build a second temple
When this new structure was erected around 520 B.C.E. , it proved initially disappointing
According to the Bible’s Book of Ezra , those who had seen the First Temple wept for sorrow since the second was a pale reflection of the first
Not that this was the only temple: There is archaeological evidence of one in Egypt in the fifth century B.C.E.; and another, even earlier, in Tel Motza , just a few miles from Solomon’s Temple
Scholars debate how temples were perceived in ancient Judah, since the Bible’s Book of Deuteronomy suggests that only the one temple in Jerusalem should exist

title: Jensen Huang’s return takes founder worship to a dangerous level
excerpt: The news of Jensen Huang’s resurrection at Nvidia felt like a practical joke or an Onion headline
body: The news of Jensen Huang’s resurrection at Nvidia felt like a practical joke or an Onion headline
Here was a cofounder and CEO of a trillion-dollar company who did just about all the bad things a CEO could do — including maybe involvement in espionage — who’d gotten his comeuppance
The investigations commenced, and Huang resigned in a rare moment of accountability in Silicon Valley culture.  But that’s not how the story ended

Huang quickly returned to the helm of Nvidia thanks to his personal friend, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, who had pressured the board to reinstate the disgraced founder. (“I made the deal,” Trump told a television audience.) When the newly vindicated CEO walked back into Nvidia headquarters on Monday, ecstatic employees cheered his name — “Jensen! Jensen!”   Considering the larger context, this is absurd

Huang is still under investigation at Nvidia, the company that he’s once again running, over his relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, who’d been talking to China’s top spy agency during the affair

And she’s under investigation over her alleged role in smuggling illegal Nvidia chips into China.  “It’s the worst degradation in corporate governance in American history and the greatest business-government scandal in US history,” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management, told me a couple of hours after the news broke. “I mean, this is crazy.” Key takeaways Silicon Valley’s founder worship started with a bad founder
In the 1950s, eight employees could no longer work for their mercurial visionary founder, so they became visionary founders themselves
Huang’s comeback shows how tech company boards still can’t control their founders
President Trump pushed Nvidia’s board to reinstate him while the company was still investigating him
Nvidia supplies the chips behind the AI boom and finances the companies buying them
When so much rides on one company, failing to hold its founder accountable can put the entire economy at risk

This is not just a matter of poor corporate governance; it is a profound collision of two visions for the future: First, there’s the founder-worshipping tradition of Silicon Valley, where visionaries not only can but should get away with anything in the name of profit and progress
Then there are the people and institutions, like the media and the government, who hold power to account and make sure this big beautiful American experiment doesn’t unravel completely
It’s not unusual for these two groups to clash
But the stakes today are higher than they’ve been in a long time

Nvidia is not only the primary supplier of chips and software to the AI boom, it’s also the industry’s chief financier, funding startups that will buy those chips and infrastructure that makes everything work
If Nvidia faltered, the whole house of cards could come down, bringing the American economy down with it
Many of the founder-worshipping class considered Huang irreplaceable , which would mean the future of the nation depended on his employment status
Jensen Huang’s restoration to his seat of power shows that Silicon Valley’s vision for the future may be winning out: The wealthiest individuals in our society operate with no baseline accountability
And even when they make colossal mistakes, their friend, the president, can restore their power.  It wasn’t supposed to be like this, but in a sense, we’ve been heading this direction for a long time
Founder worship is as old as electricity The cult of the founder lives on X these days
That’s where you could find tech leaders and venture capital types calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia and then cheering the news when it happened
Their specific arguments or grievances about Huang being pushed out seem both ridiculous and familiar (investor and podcaster Jason Calacanis seems to think that journalism is the villain here)
But beneath the rhetoric is a philosophy about the importance of an all-knowing and all-powerful tech founder that’s as old as computers and electricity itself

The tradition of worshipping the infallible founder dates back to Thomas Edison, and it’s always been central to the American tech industry, which values visionary thinking and nimble leadership above all else
You can trace the roots of this culture back to the 1950s, when a startup called Fairchild Semiconductor laid the foundation of Silicon Valley as we know it today
Fairchild made some of the first microchips, which would have made it legendary in its own right

But there was a cultural component to how the company was founded, how it was run, and what its alums went on to do that has shaped tech culture ever since.  Fairchild was actually a spinoff of another chip company, Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, founded by the co-inventor of the transistor, William Shockley
You could argue that Shockley was the original visionary founder-CEO in Silicon Valley, down to his problematic management style, which drove employees to start their own firm in 1957
Known as the “Traitorous Eight,” a group of them — including Robert Noyce, founder of Intel, and Gordon Moore, the Moore in Moore’s Law — left Shockley to start the new company
Fairchild Semiconductor got its funding and name from Fairchild Camera and Instrument, an East Coast company that thrived on military contracts for its spy satellite equipment
They eschewed the idea of letting a founder-visionary dictate its business in favor of a flat organizational structure
The pursuit of wealth is actually where you’ll find some of Nvidia’s ancestral roots
After leaving Fairchild Semiconductor, Eugene Kleiner and Don Valentine became the pioneers of modern venture capital, starting Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital, respectively in 1972
Valentine went on to fund early Silicon Valley success stories — Atari, Apple, Cisco, and Oracle, to name a few — and revered the so-called brilliant entrepreneur

According to the venture capitalist Fred Wilson, Valentine once said , “Sometimes we make money with brilliant people who are easy to get along with, most often we make money with brilliant people who are hard to get along with, but we rarely make money with normal people who are easy to get along with.” It was during Valentine’s era that we saw the cult of the founder start to form around people like Steve Jobs or Larry Ellison
Then, Sequoia Partners became the first major investor in a little chip company called Nvidia
He was actually in the room when Jensen Huang gave the original pitch in 1993
Huang apparently bombed the pitch, but Valentine invested in the venture based on the Nvidia cofounder’s reputation

The way Huang tells it , when Valentine shook his hand, he looked him square in the eye and said, “If you lose my money, I will kill you.”  At market close Monday, the day Huang was reinstated, Nvidia was worth nearly $4 trillion. “The misfits, the rebels, the troublemakers.”    The founders still worshipped in Silicon Valley have always been hailed as outsiders and disruptors

title: Jensen Huang Isn’t Worried. But You Should Be.
excerpt: The IPO was heavily oversubscribed , spurring the company to sell more shares at a higher price than it had originally intended
body: The IPO was heavily oversubscribed , spurring the company to sell more shares at a higher price than it had originally intended
The five-year-old start-up took in a record-breaking $81 billion from investors around the world, giving it a gobsmacking $1.5 trillion valuation and minting an estimated 600 centimillionaires
Nevertheless, the IPO arrived at a dour moment on Wall Street, and did not exactly brighten the mood

Investors had been selling off equities for weeks, spooked by rising interest rates, the midterm landslide, concerns about AI’s capacity to boost corporate profits, and Nvidia’s ouster of its allegedly honey-trapped CEO
When Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang yesterday, its share price surged
Then it slouched back down, joining Anthropic stock, the S&P 500, foreign-equity markets, gold, crypto, and Nasdaq in the red
The AI boom seems to be turning into an AI bust
Maybe we’ll end up thinking of it as an AI bubble
The worst possible outcome would be an AI financial crisis—and it is not a far-fetched outcome at all, given the astronomical sums, convoluted deals, and cavernous regulatory lacunae involved
The question is whether the AI whatever-it-is will play out more like the dot-com bubble of the 1990s or the housing bubble of the aughts
In the former, Nasdaq lost 78 percent of its value and the country entered a brief recession
Still, the banking system remained solvent and the credit markets liquid

In the latter, the housing market faltered, the stock market collapsed, and the entire global financial system seized, precipitating the worst recession since the Great Depression. [ Read: A shameless valley ] The difference wasn’t the amount of money at stake
The collapse of the dot-com bubble wiped out more wealth than the collapse of the housing bubble , as former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke observed in a 2012 speech
The difference was that the dot-com losses were transparent, widely distributed, and easily understood
People got excited about the World Wide Web; they bought stocks at absurd valuations; some of the companies they invested in proved to be duds; they lost money
The losses from the housing bubble, in contrast, were opaque, concentrated, and impenetrable

Where to even start? The erosion of lending standards, the explosive growth in derivatives contracts, the mispricing of mortgage-backed securities, the misguided faith in market self-regulation , the insufficient capital buffers, the regulatory gaps, the Sun Belt speculation, the low interest rates? I suppose it came down to one thing: Investors seemed like they were making a lot of different bets
But they were making one bet, on housing prices
And when that bet went sour, they panicked
However the AI story ends, it is starting the same way that the dot-com and housing stories began—with trillions of dollars

Normally, software is relatively inexpensive to develop and cheap to scale. (Mark Zuckerberg wrote most of the code for Thefacebook.com by himself in his dorm, shelling out $85 a month for a server.) But ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude Code require a tremendous amount of “compute”—basically, computing power
So AI start-ups and Silicon Valley giants are spending $600 billion this year alone on silicon chips and data-center construction
They are issuing shares, as Anthropic did last week
They’re selling bonds: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle issued $223 billion in debt in the first eight months of the year
They are also making arrangements with private creditors
Here’s where things start to feel very 1996
The markets are making a massive wager on AI revolutionizing the business world, just as they made a massive wager on the World Wide Web revolutionizing the business world
The value of AI-related stocks has climbed $27 trillion since the launch of ChatGPT, according to Goldman Sachs
Even given the recent correction, the country is in the midst of a hell of a bull market
Yet the markets are making that bet on the basis of some awfully rosy assumptions
By 2031, AI-linked companies will need to generate $6 trillion a year in revenue to justify the cost of the build-out , according to calculations by the consultancy Bain & Company
That is six times as much as American businesses and households spend on gasoline and other petroleum products each year, to give a sense of scale
It is eight times as much as U.S. firms shell out for software
It’s more than the country spends on health care
AI revenue seems highly likely to fall short of expectations, while AI overhead costs seem highly likely to exceed them
Anthropic is committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on compute in the coming years
And many AI firms have hefty borrowing costs to deal with, as well as hefty infrastructure costs

CoreWeave, an AI cloud-computing firm, is spending a quarter of its revenue servicing its loans. [ Read: The economy is a hostage situation ] The disconnect between the two sides of the balance sheet is making the markets feel bearish
Some AI companies are having a harder time raising the cash they need to refine and run their algorithms

title: A Good Gift Is More Ordinary Than You Think
excerpt: This is an edition of Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s guide to making everyday life vivid
body: This is an edition of Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s guide to making everyday life vivid
The holidays are the worst time to give a gift
Chocolate or socks received on a random Wednesday in August would be incredible; the same socks on Father’s Day or chocolate on Valentine’s Day veer toward cliché
A gift is a paradox: As it becomes more socially expected, it also becomes harder to give well
I learned to give gifts from my late mother, who was terrible at gift giving no matter the time of year
She would agree to buy a specific thing for my kids but renege at the last minute, for mysterious reasons
Or she’d ask for the kids’ clothing sizes, then send garments in different ones
Once, she bought me a new set of flatware—nice!—but not in sufficient quantity to actually supply the kitchen, so I had to buy more to make the gift useful
Over the years, my wife received innumerable scarves and folk-art objects that matched Mom’s tastes but not her own
Mom didn’t mean to be terrible at gift giving, and I now understand her effort as a struggle rather than a slight
She seemed to recognize that she couldn’t conceptualize the desires of other people
Often, she tried to make up for that deficiency with sheer volume
A birthday parcel would contain lots of little junk—the kind of stuff you’d collect as trade-show swag
Each delivered the earnest desire to make a gift connect, along with the tragedy of connection’s failure
In the end, by getting the practice so wrong, Mom gave me the gift of understanding gifts better
The best gifts give something greater than any one thing: the message that you know the recipient in a nuanced and personal way
To give well is first to see, and to receive well is to allow yourself to be seen
Over time, people have developed ways to reduce gift giving’s burden: Wish lists, for example, were once limited to kids but now cross generations
Telling someone else exactly what you want is good, in that it disambiguates desire
But it also frees a person from the difficult work that can make a gift truly meaningful
Think about the people closest to you—your spouse or children or parents, for example
You know so much about them, but when it comes to thinking of a gift, you might find yourself stumped
I could try to learn about yarn or yarn-wrangling tools, and doing so might connect me to her through a deeper understanding of her interests
When I think about my own hobbies and avocations—home espresso and gelato, for example—I closely guard my tools and materials and don’t want someone else getting involved
Similarly, my adult son is really into photography, and because of that passion I know that he already owns a version of almost anything I might think of
Setting aside the most obvious interests of your gift recipient can help avoid this mess
But doing so makes giving a gift even harder, because now you must find an even less apparent feature of the other person to develop into an opportunity for communion

Unfortunately, this is where many people settle on options from the gift-guide mainstay, “the person who has everything.” That usually means things nobody wants or needs—superfluous curiosities such as a neck massager or an electric gravy warmer
An indulgent or expensive gift might also not fit the bill
You might feel formidable or magnanimous when you give a lavish gift, but receiving one can be disquieting
Or, if a wish list is on offer, it might entice you to choose a variation on the category of item listed
Do not do this; this is very bad. (Everyone remembers getting the wrong version of the popular toy as a kid.) Understandably, you will want to make your mark on their wishes
But the best gift is not about you at all—not even your generosity in the giving
A gift entails the attempt to set yourself aside as much as possible, and to wrap a bow around the most nuanced and tender understanding of someone else that you can muster
Think back over the past year or so, and try to recall when your gift recipient may have revealed a desire, problem, aspiration, or fact that felt distinctive
I’m not talking about a specific yearning for a consumer good, although that is one option
I mean a moment that, when revisited, reveals something fundamental about their current self
Focus on the most ordinary events and encounters, the ones even the person on your mind may not remember
Those moments can offer the richest information about what makes someone who they are
Perhaps a friend delighted at a specific jam served at a brunch out

title: The Agents Howard Lutnick Pulled off Their Jobs
excerpt: E arly in his tenure , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick so alienated members of his regular security detail that some of them quit
body: E arly in his tenure , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick so alienated members of his regular security detail that some of them quit
He didn’t have to look far for replacements
The Department of Commerce’s own Bureau of Industry and Security employs law-enforcement agents who carry weapons and have the power to arrest people
The department reassigned some of them to serve as Lutnick’s personal bodyguards, pulling away from their duties agents who might otherwise have prevented the smuggling of AI chips to China
Instead, they would now travel on his private jet and guard his various homes, according to five people with knowledge of the matter
Some commerce officials were baffled that Lutnick had diverted personnel for his own protection as the United States is racing to stay ahead of China on advanced artificial intelligence
BIS is the nation’s leading bureau for the enforcement of export controls, and its agents are trained to keep prized U.S. technology out of the wrong hands

In theory, they should be on the front lines of the effort to prevent illicit AI-chip trading—the issue at the center of the controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. (Huang has admitted to the affair but said that he hadn’t known that the woman might have been a Chinese spy.) BIS agents are trained in many aspects of law enforcement, including crime-scene investigation and counterterrorism
They are not, however, trained in protecting VIPs and dignitaries
The Commerce Department has its own Office of Security, and secretaries have been provided with protection since at least 1986
But that protection has traditionally been lighter than what’s provided to senior officials who are more closely involved in national security, who are considered more likely targets

The assignment of BIS agents as bodyguards, former officials told us, seemed driven by Lutnick’s desire to have a detail comparable to that of other Cabinet members, such as the secretary of defense and the attorney general

Democrats and some Republicans have questioned why Lutnick hasn’t done more to prevent illegal sales of advanced chips from Nvidia and other firms, or expanded the list of companies that are barred on national-security grounds from making such purchases

In particular, lawmakers want to know more about Lutnick’s approach to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that’s under investigation by Commerce and the Justice Department for potential chip smuggling

Even after U.S. intelligence, about a year ago, identified the Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as a Chinese-intelligence asset who was in a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the Commerce Department didn’t put Megaspeed on its trade blacklist
The company was added only yesterday, the same day that Nvidia’s board restored Jensen Huang to his roles as the company’s president and chief executive, under pressure from President Trump

The belated addition to the blacklist appears to have been more symbolic than substantive, however: One trade expert suggested that because of the way the regulation adding Megaspeed to the list was written, the company would still have access to many types of AI chips
T he Bureau of Industry and Security has fewer than 200 special agents; most of them work in 10 field offices across the United States, and about a dozen or so work overseas
It wasn’t clear how many agents were affected by the rotations onto and off Lutnick’s protection staff
Two former officials told us that the assignment usually involved three to four agents at a time

A Commerce Department official said in a statement that “at a time when the Secretary was facing the highest level of credible threats in the Department’s history some agents were temporarily detailed to augment executive protection.” The official added that the number of agents at BIS has increased, though she didn’t provide numbers
As artificial intelligence has boomed, the bureau has struggled to keep pace with the global trade in U.S. chips, suggesting that it could ill-afford the secondment of agents elsewhere
The Commerce Department’s Office of the Inspector General, in a June report, found that BIS has not taken adequate action to enforce export controls on goods destined for China and Hong Kong

In a report a month earlier, it found similar enforcement failures regarding Russia and Belarus. [ Read: The limits of positive thinking ] Overall, the number of public penalties and enforcement actions for violating U.S.-export rules has fallen since Lutnick took office in February 2025

Across 2023 and 2024, the annual case rate was close to 100; in the 17 months from March 2025 to the start of August, the annualized rate dropped to about half that, according to The Export Practitioner , a trade publication
Amid the furor over Nvidia, the inspector general last week began an evaluation of the bureau’s oversight of advanced-computing chips
Current and former commerce officials we spoke with put the blame for the bureau’s lackluster performance on Lutnick and his team
They contend that Lutnick and senior officials have repeatedly stressed Trump’s interest in a détente with China and have placed commercial interests above national security
Trump has made clear his desire for a new China trade deal and last week sought to further improve relations with President Xi Jinping at a summit in Shenzhen
Trump’s approach runs counter to the administration’s aggressive posturing about the need to restrict Chinese trade

The diversion of agents to serve in Lutnick’s protective detail has sapped expert resources and prevented agents from doing the high-stakes work they are hired and trained to perform, current and former officials told us. “They’re not trained for protective detail,” one current official told us. “These are professional investigators.” A former official called it “completely inappropriate” to pull agents to protect Lutnick
The Commerce Department, meanwhile, is seeking an increase in staffing

In April, Lutnick told the House Appropriations Subcommittee that BIS needed additional resources and enforcement personnel, including 290 new enforcement officers, to prevent the diversion of semiconductors to China and to protect American innovation
He didn’t mention the redeployment of some of the officers whom BIS already employed
L utnick , a friend of Trump’s and a former Wall Street executive, is one of the Cabinet’s wealthiest members
His most recent financial-disclosure form lists his holdings, which include a $25 million mansion that he purchased in 2024 in the Berkley neighborhood of Washington, D.C
The house, modeled after France’s Château du Grand-Lucé, was until recently the most expensive home ever sold in the capital
Lutnick also owns properties in New York City, the Hamptons, and South Florida
He made much of his money as the CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York financial firm, where his two sons, Brandon and Kyle, hold senior leadership positions

Cantor also held approximately 1.8 million Nvidia shares as of the end of June, which were valued at the time at $362 million, according to the company’s financial disclosures. (The firm has said that it has no material proprietary position in Nvidia, and its holdings mainly arise from its services for clients.) [ Read: The president’s most annoying buddy ] Lutnick no longer has a financial interest in Cantor Fitzgerald, but some in Congress have argued that his close family ties to the firm represent a conflict of interest

title: What It Means to Secure Elections
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The relatively smooth functioning of the midterms did not end President Trump’s thr
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts The relatively smooth functioning of the midterms did not end President Trump’s threat to American election integrity
After initially accepting the results, Trump has begun calling them into question, and House Republicans have named the outspoken 2020-election denier Jim Jordan as their next leader
Ensuring a free and fair 2028 presidential election and a peaceful transition of power remain pressing concerns for anyone who wants the country back on solidly democratic footing

In this episode of Autocracy in America , the Democratic election lawyer and founder of Democracy Docket Marc Elias speaks about his work safeguarding the midterms, the continued threats to our democratic system, and why restoring the Voting Rights Act won’t be enough to solve our problems
The following is a transcript of the episode: Anne Applebaum: I’m Anne Applebaum
We’ve just had the most consequential midterm elections in modern history
Americans clearly voted for a different kind of government
But major change will require more than one election

In this season, we will ask what steps need to be taken to undo the damage the Trump presidencies have done to our political system and reverse the slide to autocracy, even as Trump himself remains in office
At the center of any functioning democracy is the right to vote
A representative government is only truly representative if it somehow reflects the will of the people
The surest sign of a failing democracy, by contrast, is a flawed, manipulated voting process or one that always produces contested results
Americans have been trying to manipulate their voting system for decades
The word gerrymander was invented in 1812 when then–Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry drew a voting district that resembled a salamander
During the Jim Crow years, some American states wrote laws deliberately designed to prevent Black people from voting
Other states have tried to make it harder for students or poor people to vote by limiting polling stations or creating obstacles to voter registration
But since the beginning of the second Trump term, the federal government for the first time became the most important source of voter suppression, not the states
Having urged supporters to attack the Capitol in order to block Joe Biden from becoming president in 2021, Donald Trump did his best to shape the result of these elections in advance
He used government funds to make election advertisements
He sought to pass legislation that would make voting more difficult, and he tried to use the U.S
Postal Service to restrict mail voting by obliging the service to determine who receives a mail ballot
His Justice Department sued multiple states in an attempt to gain control over lists of voters, and they lost all of those suits
To talk about the 2026 elections and to reflect on how we can build a stronger electoral system in the future, I have invited Marc Elias
He and his law firm have represented dozens of U.S. politicians as well as U.S. voters in cases involving campaign finance, voting rights, and redistricting
He’s also a strong advocate of voting rights and of high voter participation. [ Music ] Marc Elias, thanks for joining me
Applebaum: Since the election, quite a few people have remarked on how smooth it seemed to be
There were no overt attempts to prevent people from voting, as many had feared there would be

I’d like to start by asking you about the work that went into that smoothness and into that success: What were people doing to prepare for the midterm vote? Elias: So first of all, there’s no question we had a free and fair election
But I think it can be overstated that there were no obstacles for people to vote and that the government and other actors did not do things to try to make it harder to vote and easier to cheat

After all, we had an unprecedented effort by the Trump administration to actually prevent, among other things, mail-in voting, to try to prevent California from tabulating all of their ballots, to try to prevent Alaska from certifying the election results if a Democrat wins
So the fact that those things failed are good for democracy, but I think everyone needs to keep in mind that those things were tried and didn’t succeed
Now, in answer to your question, what we do, the way I think about preparing for Election Day is you try to solve the big systemic problems and then the small local problems
What made 2026 kind of a unique election in that it was actually the federal government rather than the states who were posing some of the greatest risks to elections
And then at a local level, we are involved in a lot of litigation and a lot of working with candidates and local election officials to try to remove the friction points

Those friction points can be a surge in provisional ballots, in people having their polling places closed, and those things can make a real difference, not just to individual voters and obviously to communities, but also to the outcomes of elections
Applebaum: And tell me what you were doing in Mississippi, because I know you were there in the days after the voting, or your organization was there

When you say you’re going down there to protect the vote, what are you doing? What’s necessary to do after an election to make sure the votes are counted correctly, and how can grassroots organizations or legal groups help? Elias: Anne, I’ll be honest with you
In the 1990s, I picked up an odd specialty of close elections, which, at the time, did not seem like a growth industry
I was involved in Harry Reid’s recount in 1998
I was part of the legal team for Maria Cantwell in 2000, so I wasn’t in Florida

title: Was a Drug Lord’s Killing in Ecuador Not What It Seemed?
excerpt: T he pictures show men splayed on a highway, their faces concealed in pools of blood
body: T he pictures show men splayed on a highway, their faces concealed in pools of blood
An assault rifle lying by one man’s outstretched hands

Ecuadorean Defense Minister Gian Carlo Loffredo posted the grisly images as proof of his country’s deepening partnership with the Trump administration in its campaign against drug cartels in Latin America
The photos, he said on social media two months ago, stemmed from an operation conducted in cooperation with U.S

Southern Command. “We promised: ‘Jail or hell’ and this one didn’t make it to jail,” Loffredo wrote on X on September 23, saying that the target was a cartel leader known as “Charlie.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth reposted Loffredo’s message the same day, adding that the U.S. military was “proud to stand w/ the Armed Forces of Ecuador.” But the Trump administration is now investigating whether Ecuadorean forces committed crimes or human-rights abuses during that operation—including whether the suspects were killed while in Ecuadorean custody—and whether U.S. forces played any role, one senior administration official and one former official told us
While administration officials look into the raid, the U.S. military has suspended joint operations with Ecuadorean troops, one of the people familiar with the matter said

But the U.S. military has not stopped its push to embed itself in Ecuador’s fight against cartels. (Hegseth visited the country last week.) Ecuador is Exhibit A of the Trump administration’s expanding militarized campaign to strike powerful drug and other criminal groups in Latin America in partnership with Donald Trump–aligned right-wing governments
Stephen Miller , Trump’s longtime immigration adviser, has driven that effort
Miller met with Ecuadorean President Daniel Noboa the day before the “Charlie” raid, while Noboa was in New York to address the United Nations General Assembly

With Miller’s recent appointment as White House chief of staff, those in Trump’s orbit are preparing for an escalation of U.S.-military operations in Latin America in the coming weeks and months. “This is all Stephen’s thing,” the senior official said, referring to the expanding partnerships. “This would not have happened without Stephen.” The U.S. military has forces in Ecuador to train and advise local troops and conduct what it calls “partnered operations”—joint raids or other counter-drug missions

A Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the department, told us in an emailed statement that U.S.-military personnel did not take part in the September 23 operation, but declined to provide further details or comment about any review
But officials are still working to establish whether U.S. forces provided intelligence assistance or any other kind of support to the operation, sources told us

The Defense Department “takes allegations of misconduct by our partners seriously,” the Pentagon official said. “The Department remains committed to working alongside sovereign partners, including Ecuador, to confront narco-terrorist networks, strengthen collective security, and defend our shared neighborhood.” Officials from Ecuador’s embassy in Washington did not provide comment before publication

A White House official told us in an email that the drug gangs that the United States is battling alongside Latin American allies represent “a clear and present danger” to U.S. security, and said that the actions taken under those partnerships “have saved countless lives.” The official added that, at the time, Miller served as the homeland-security adviser and was responsible for interagency coordination. “The Trump Administration is the first administration in history to adopt a comprehensive strategy to dismantle and defeat narco-terrorists that are responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Americans,” the official wrote
When we asked the White House which agency or agencies were leading the examination of the raid, it didn’t respond
T rump in his second term has taken a special interest in Latin America, a region that has been largely overlooked by U.S. policy makers in recent decades
The administration wants to choke off the flow of migrants and drugs

That has brought a Trumpian corollary to the Monroe Doctrine—which the president proudly calls the “Donroe Doctrine,” a modern version of the 19th-century principle that the Western Hemisphere must remain under American influence
Miller’s vision for combatting cartels has expanded accordingly

He is a principal architect of the administration’s campaign of missile strikes against suspected drug traffickers at sea, which legal experts and critics have said is likely illegal. (The White House has cited a classified opinion from the Office of Legal Counsel that it insists authorizes the strikes.) The campaign has killed at least 240 people in more than 70 air strikes since last fall, according to a tally of Pentagon announcements

Some of those attacks have occurred in the Caribbean, the military has said, but the majority are in the eastern Pacific, where there have also been a number of interdictions off the coast of Ecuador. [ Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’ ] The administration has at times been willing to overlook its Latin American partners’ records on human rights and democracy, depicting the battle against criminal groups as an existential struggle for all in the region. “You have to make a choice here

We’re going to choose on the side of leaders that are going to be serious about taking these groups on and eliminating them once and for all,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Ecuador earlier this year. “Otherwise, those groups—those terrorist groups—will eat these countries up.” The U.S. military touted its relationship with Ecuador in March when it announced the launch of joint operations against cartels
Noboa has put addressing rampant criminality and violence at the center of his presidency
He is among the most public of Trump’s Latin American allies in courting U.S.-military involvement

In his own social-media post within hours of the September raid, Noboa echoed the White House’s view of the fight against cartels as a hemisphere-wide campaign against criminality. “This battle doesn’t end at our borders,” he wrote
The slain cartel leader known as “Charlie” was Carlos Germán Muñoz Jara, according to Ecuadorean media
He was believed to have links to the Ecuadorean gang Los Choneros and the Mexican cartel Jalisco Nueva Generación
The Trump administration has designated both groups foreign terrorist organizations
The administration’s campaign is not limited to Ecuador

It is also seeking to accelerate counter-drug operations with Colombia, historically the most important U.S.-military partner in the region, and Venezuela following the January ouster of the dictator Nicolás Maduro
Hegseth visited Bogotá and Caracas last week to tout expanded military cooperation
The administration’s desire to intensify counter-cartel operations in Mexico, potentially on a unilateral basis, has caused friction between Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum

Mexico captured a top drug boss, El Chapo Isidro, last week, in a sign of Sheinbaum’s determination to show Washington that her country is taking action. [ Read: Claudia Sheinbaum’s impossible dilemma ] Ecuador has approved a dramatic expansion of the U.S. military’s role in the country, including joint operations and the positioning of U.S. troops on the ground to train and advise their Ecuadorean counterparts
At least two MQ-9 Reaper drones are now based in Ecuador, along with other equipment provided by the United States
Noboa has faced accusations of authoritarian tactics employed against political opponents
Human Rights Watch alleged in a report that a March Ecuadorean military raid had resulted in the torture of farm workers
Ecuadoreans have put some limits on Noboa’s efforts, rejecting a 2025 referendum that would have permitted U.S. military bases in the country
Ecuador’s counter-drug partnership with the United States goes beyond the military
In recent months, the Drug Enforcement Administration, FBI, and Department of Homeland Security have also supported the country’s efforts
With the Pentagon and White House pushing for more military action against narco-terrorists, U.S. troops are likely to be busy in Latin America

title: He Thought About Rome Every Day
excerpt: The year was 1764, and Edward Gibbon was 27, headed for Rome on his Grand Tour
body: The year was 1764, and Edward Gibbon was 27, headed for Rome on his Grand Tour

He had traversed the Alps from France not on a mule but in a chair carried between poles by porters. (He was “no great jockey,” a companion noted.) Gibbon then made his way through Turin and Milan, paused in Florence, and, as autumn set in, continued south

Crossing the Tiber, his destination now in sight, he was overcome. “I can neither express nor forget the strong emotions which agitated my mind as I first approached and entered the eternal city,” Gibbon recalled years later in a memoir. “After a sleepless night I trod, with a lofty step, the ruins of the Forum; each memorable spot where Romulus stood or Tully spoke or Caesar fell was at once present to my eye; and several days of intoxication were lost or enjoyed before I could descend to a cool and minute investigation.” Gibbon loved his rhetorical couplings—those harnessed pairs of verbs or adjectives that are sometimes at odds (“lost or enjoyed,” “express nor forget”), pulling the reader in different directions, as the critic Clive James once observed

The oddest pairing of all is that of Gibbon himself and his monumental work, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire , which he began writing seven years after that first (and only) visit to Rome
Gibbon was, by his own description, “puny”—4 feet 7 inches tall
His masterpiece is towering, a million and a half words published over the course of little more than a decade
The first of the six volumes—an immediate best seller in Britain—appeared the same year as the Declaration of Independence and The Wealth of Nations
There was no real precedent for what Gibbon had achieved
The Decline and Fall was an attempt to write history in a way we now take for granted : that is, by seeking to explain what actually happened
Gibbon was neither an annalist nor a zealot

He had arguments to make—about the unrivaled stability and happiness enjoyed for a spell by the Roman empire’s subjects, about the defeat of liberty by despotism and decadence, about the corrosive effects of corruption and Christianity—but his account is not subservient to them
He is often imprecise, as well as confident in his imagination
Gibbon’s appetite for written sources was gargantuan and his knowledge of them profound, though he did not bring a modern critical faculty to their interpretation
He was an impresario, not a pedant—judicious, skeptical, and ironic, with a taste for drama

And the writing! At times so over-egged as to make Henry James seem like Hemingway, but seductive in its rhythms and illuminated by epigrammatic flashes: “A good soldier should dread his own officers far more than the enemy.” “Revenge is profitable, gratitude is expensive.” The narrative is at once sweeping and detailed—equal parts Balzac and Trollope, George Lucas and TMZ
The Decline and Fall ’s influence has been immense

The work created the basic storyline of Roman history , from “good emperors” to barbarians, and for generations has shaped an understanding of imperial ruin as “the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness.” It captivated newly independent America, whose Founders cherished republican government but feared that the Roman past held danger signs

People continue to explore its claims and insights, as well as the experiences that shaped its author: Was Gibbon a fatalist or, living at the core of a young empire himself , an optimist? Whatever the answer, his eyes seem to follow us around the room

Gibbon the man is a figure, as Martha Saxton writes in her posthumously published The Conversions of Edward Gibbon: A Modern Biography , who appears almost laughably devoid of the majesty his prose leads you to expect
As a boy, his ungainly body and unhappy experiences with peers left him deeply insecure and drove him to books
In later life, he grew obese and suffered from a hydrocele—a scrotal swelling—that further hampered his movement
He was vain and foppish, with a habit of waving his snuffbox didactically when he wanted to make a point
People acknowledged his brilliance but also made him an object of ridicule and even contempt

James Boswell, who knew Gibbon as a member of the Club, a literary group that included Samuel Johnson, described him as an “ugly, affected, disgusting fellow.” Saxton, a feminist historian and for many years a professor at Amherst College, is the author of acclaimed biographies of Jayne Mansfield, Louisa May Alcott, and Mary Ball Washington (the mother of George)
She came to Gibbon from an unusual angle, her attention drawn initially by the notable misogyny of the Decline and Fall
Powerful women are painted as gorgons or succubi
The few whom Gibbon approves of are described as possessing “manly” virtues
In Gibbon’s lexicon, decadence is often a synonym for effeminacy
But Saxton’s response to Gibbon is complicated
She describes herself as both repelled by his venom and dazzled by the Decline and Fall —by its writing, scope, and command, and by the mark it left
She also finds Gibbon’s misogyny baffling
Male writers of the Enlightenment were eager to engage a female audience

Gibbon himself enjoyed close friendships with several women, in particular an aunt, Catherine Porten, who first cultivated “a taste for books, which is still the pleasure and glory of my life.” Aunt Kitty would be Gibbon’s friend and counselor for nearly four decades
Saxton doesn’t have a ready explanation for Gibbon’s attitudes, and doesn’t try to force one
Instead, she broadens her inquiry to explore the inner life of a man who repeatedly broke with convention—the “conversions” of her title—only to scramble back to safer ground
A lonely misfit emerges from her book, confident in his abilities but wounded in his soul, who escapes into a world of words as the only place where he can exercise complete control

Saxton is hardly protective of her subject, but she also has no patience for the cruelty of men like Boswell, whose remarks about Gibbon give her “much sympathy for the tiny, affected, brilliant, scarred man.” [ From the January 1878 issue: William Dean Howells on Edward Gibbon ] Gibbon was born in South London in 1737 to a family of wealth and property
Though sickly himself, he was the only one of seven children to survive infancy
His difficult father was a stern traditionalist who kept a tight hold on money and behavior
The most significant event from Gibbon’s brief time at Oxford was his rebellious embrace of Catholicism—not a route to advancement in 18th-century Britain

title: Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization
excerpt: Enterprise networks are under severe strain
body: Enterprise networks are under severe strain
As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network
Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows
As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening
As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty
Key findings from the report include: AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads
Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users
Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements
AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises
Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical
Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows

Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure
AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways
The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure
Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease

A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time
Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades
NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations
Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises.  Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders

This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations

It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
excerpt: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants
body: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants
Over 100 such facilities have been announced in the US since early 2025, with combined capacity exceeding 115 gigawatts
A dirtier shortcut: If all planned US projects proceed, they could emit 152 million metric tons more CO₂ annually than if those data centers were grid connected, according to BloombergNEF tracking

Fossil fuel lock-in is a real risk: Though developers pitch private gas plants as temporary bridges until grid connections come through, experts warn that once built, operators are unlikely to simply switch them off—potentially cementing decades of fossil fuel dependency
Everyone else pays the price: Going off-grid doesn't insulate communities from the fallout

Greater natural gas demand could drive up fuel prices, squeezing the roughly 60% of American households that rely on it for heating and cooking. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149622" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade

Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.   xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024
At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators
It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles
But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company
The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California
The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025
It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today
But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy
When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator

That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability
Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them
Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants

These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup. “This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation
Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however

Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.  Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.  The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions
Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation

That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)  Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand

Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.  Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines
These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build
Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says

That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.  BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US

If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report

That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.  And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation
More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking
That effect may also trickle into electricity prices
There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone
Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data
Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says

Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.  While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds

In a recent study , his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels. “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”
