<title>Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773898/original/file-20261110-64-9pmqkq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=1999%2C0%2C5769%2C3846&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Prevention is currently the only way to contain the disease, which has seen a resurgence in the number of cases since September, particularly in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unlimphotos.com/92521652/mpox-hands-with-monkeypox-rash-outbreak-of-the-mpxv-virus-infectious-disease-spreading.html">Berit/Unlimphotos</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The city of Rio de Janeiro has <a href="https://epirio.svs.rio.br/painel/mpox/">reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox</a>, an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026. </p>

<p>Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.</p>

<p>The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, <a href="https://prefeitura.sp.gov.br/documents/d/saude/boletim_mpox_17_11_2026-publicar-pdf">128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17</a>, which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year. </p>

<p>The national figures are not alarming: <a href="https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/composicao/svsa/cnie/painel-mpox">1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23</a>, compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022. </p>

<p>The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.</p>

<p>In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.</p>

<p>In response, the Ministry of Health <a href="https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/2026/novembro/mpox-ministerio-da-saude-garante-25-mil-doses-de-vacina-apos-negociacao-internacional">purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease</a> and instructed states and municipalities to <a href="https://simplenursing.com/intradermal-injection/">administer it intradermally</a> – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.</p>

<p>The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just <a href="https://www.healio.com/news/infectious-disease/20250317/tecovirimat-fails-to-reduce-clade-ii-mpox-lesions-pain-viral-clearance">failed two clinical trials</a>.</p>

<h2>What has changed about the virus?</h2>

<p>Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to <a href="https://www.who.int/news/item/14-08-2024-who-director-general-declares-mpox-outbreak-a-public-health-emergency-of-international-concern">declare an international public health emergency</a> in August 2024.</p>

<p>Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.</p>

<p>At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, <a href="https://fiocruz.br/noticia/2026/11/ini-fiocruz-e-unidade-de-referencia-para-atendimento-de-casos-de-mpox">43 of the 62 samples</a> identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.</p>

<p>Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.</p>

<p>Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first <a href="https://agenciaaids.com.br/noticias/aumento-de-casos-de-mpox-no-rio-de-janeiro-e-preciso-reconhecer-que-estamos-diante">cases with evidence of community transmission</a> – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.</p>

<p>The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.</p>

<p>In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.</p>

<h2>Antiviral drug failed the test</h2>

<p>During the 2022 outbreak, the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/monkeypox/hcp/clinical-care/tecovirimat.html">antiviral drug tecovirimat</a> was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been <a href="https://www.coc.fiocruz.br/pesquisa/historia-das-ciencias-e-da-saude/claudio-amaral-e-a-erradicacao-da-variola/">eradicated from the planet since 1980</a>. But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.</p>

<p>An April 2025 trial <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2412439">compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo</a> in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.</p>

<p>In February 2026, a second trial <a href="https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2506495">settled the question regarding clade II</a>. The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.</p>

<p>Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="red bumps on a forearm" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=336&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=336&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=336&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771181/original/file-20261110-64-mycsj9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=423&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unlimphotos.com/61759126/male-arm-with-red-pustules-monkeypox.html">Olga Gubskaya/Unlimphotos</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What the vaccine does</h2>

<p>The only vaccine for mpox is <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/monkeypox/vaccines/index.html">MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos</a>, a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, <a href="https://doi.org/10.4187/respcare.11170">observational studies</a> conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.</p>

<p>Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that <a href="https://www.who.int/news-room/public-advice/mpox-vaccination">this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two</a>, compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39413490/">ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses</a>.</p>

<p>In the U.S., a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines12060651">estimated 89% protection</a> with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose.</p>

<p>In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(25)00018-0">only 35% among people living with HIV</a> – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection.</p>

<h2>Weak points</h2>

<p>There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels <a href="https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.09.10.24313399">drop sharply between six and 12 months</a> after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection.</p>

<p>The second is that there is no data on clinical efficacy against clade Ib, though there are laboratory studies. A British group showed in April 2026 that <a href="https://www.thepandemicinstitute.org/news/study-shows-mpox-vaccine-generates-immune-response-to-emerging-clade-ib-but-protection-levels-remain-unclear/">serum from 25 vaccinated healthcare workers neutralizes clade Ib</a>, but at levels consistently lower than those observed against clade IIb. Cross-protection is likely, based on animal models challenged with clade I. The extent of this protection in humans, however, is unknown.</p>

<p>The intradermal injection method, now recommended by Brazil’s Ministry of Health, was adopted in the United States and Europe in 2022 – this method allows the use of one-fifth of the dose – and produced an immune response comparable to that of the subcutaneous method. The costs associated with the vaccine include personnel training and vials of the vaccine that, once thawed, must be used within four weeks.</p>

<h2>The ministry’s decision</h2>

<p>Right now, prevention is the only way to contain mpox.</p>

<p>The purchase of vaccines for Brazil was made through the Pan American Health Organization Revolving Fund. The initial order of 20,000 doses was <a href="https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/saude/noticia/2026-11/ministerio-informa-ter-adquirido-25-mil-doses-de-vacina-contra-mpox">increased to 25,000</a> following negotiations with the manufacturer, with distribution <a href="https://g1.globo.com/sp/sao-paulo/noticia/2026/11/23/mpox-vacina-contra-a-doenca-comeca-a-ser-distribuida-em-sp-nesta-segunda-veja-quem-pode-tomar.ghtml">scheduled to begin Nov. 23</a>.</p>

<p>Prior to that, 3,650 doses from the national stockpile had already been shipped to nine states, including Rio de Janeiro, Ceará and the Federal District. The Unified Health System is limiting vaccination to specific groups: people living with HIV, users of preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, laboratory professionals who handle the virus, and medium- or high-risk contacts of confirmed cases. In line with WHO guidelines, there is no mass plan for vaccination. Vaccinations are administered at immunization reference centers rather than primary care clinics.</p>

<p>This decision is based on epidemiological logic and a practical constraint – the global shortage of the vaccine. But the bottleneck in Brazil has not always been supply. Between 2022 and 2023, the country <a href="https://doi.org/10.1590/0102-311XPT006624">distributed 49,000 doses of the mpox vaccine and administered 14,395</a> – less than a third. </p>

<p>In a survey of more than 9,500 people of different sexual orientations and gender identities, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jia2.70143">only 4.9% reported having received at least one dose</a>. The researchers pointed to limited availability and barriers to access as likely explanations for the low coverage.</p>

<p>These same factors are likely to determine whether the 25,000 new doses will make a difference. To protect those at risk before exposure, the vaccine must reach these individuals in time for them to complete the two-dose regimen. This will require that the vaccine be available at facilities that offer PrEP for HIV and at the sexual health clinics these patients already attend – not just at public hospitals where they are unlikely to go.</p>

<p>In the meantime, the Ministry of Health is encouraging anyone who develops new skin lesions – especially if accompanied by a fever or swollen lymph nodes – to seek medical care and avoid close physical contact until they have been evaluated. They are also encouraging people with HIV to keep their antiretroviral therapy up to date, because immunosuppression, rather than the clade, determines who becomes severely ill with mpox.</p>

This version has been updated to reflect new case numbers at the time of publication.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297434/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?

<title>What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773737/original/file-20261123-62-op3d0l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=147%2C0%2C5704%2C3802&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Nvidia&#39;s chips have put the company at the center of the AI boom.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/the-sign-outside-the-nvidia-corporation-office-building-news-photo/2304900983">Stephen J. Boitano/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster <a href="https://apnews.com/article/nvidia-jensen-huang-39d4b34ffaa867b4e669893b5fd5028f">and reinstatement</a>, the central role of Nvidia <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/the-nvidia-scandal-is-heightening-americas-ai-rivalry-with-china-ahead-of-trumps-visit">in the U.S.-China AI competition</a>, and the U.S. economy’s <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/the-ai-boom-is-transforming-the-american-economy-beyond-recognition-c7825b31">reliance on the AI boom</a> might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?</p>

<p>The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.</p>

<p>GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=QmOVGRAAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">researcher of high-performance computing</a> and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.</p>

<h2>GPUs vs. CPUs</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.howtogeek.com/694869/what-is-a-cpu-and-what-does-it-do/">The CPU</a> is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, <a href="https://www.howtogeek.com/702766/what-is-a-gpu-graphics-processing-units-explained/">a GPU</a> typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.</p>

<p>A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform <a href="https://spectrum.ieee.org/generative-ai-training">more than a quadrillion</a>, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9HDQH6ReAyw?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The Financial Times lays out how Nvidia came to dominate the AI chip market.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>From pretty pictures to AI data centers</h2>

<p>Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia <a href="https://qz.com/nvidia-history-graphics-cards-ai-boom#the-1999-ipo-and-the-geforce-256">dominated the market</a> for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.</p>

<p>In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/1015706.1015800">software tools</a> that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.</p>

<p>The second major shift occurred when <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3065386">AlexNet</a>, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work. </p>

<p>Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.</p>

<p>Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads. </p>

<h2>AI takes off</h2>

<p>In 2017, Google researchers <a href="https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3295222.3295349">introduced the transformer</a>, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.</p>

<p>The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models. </p>

<p>These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns. </p>

<h2>AI ‘arms race’</h2>

<p>Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/rare-nvidias-record-profit-margin-164824665.html">record profits for Nvidia</a>, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. <p>Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-supercharges-data-center-energy-use-straining-the-grid-and-slowing-sustainability-efforts-232697">enormous amounts of electricity</a>, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities. </p>

<p>The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/15/nvidia-apple-broadcom-in-fierce-battle-to-make-chips-at-tsmc.html">fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant</a> Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-data-center-boom-is-leaving-consumer-electronics-short-of-chips-even-though-they-dont-use-the-same-kinds-277069">strained supplies of memory chips</a>, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones. </p>

<p>Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/297128/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering

CPUs The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time
In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel
A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI
Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over
Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion , or thousand trillion, of these operations every second
The Financial Times lays out how Nvidia came to dominate the AI chip market
From pretty pictures to AI data centers Early GPUs could only draw graphics
Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel
Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s
In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations
That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007

<title>Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773621/original/file-20261123-62-cseomn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5712%2C3808&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Climate%20El%20Nino/8465583f09a748c8810aa63fa03b6dcf/photo">AP Photo/Charlie Riedel</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño <a href="https://theconversation.com/floridas-flooding-deja-vu-is-a-sign-of-things-to-come-so-who-is-most-at-risk-and-how-can-they-prepare-297006">has caused flooding</a> in low-lying Florida communities, <a href="https://theconversation.com/california-is-taking-a-beating-from-an-unusually-destructive-2026-pacific-hurricane-season-294207">hammered the California coast</a> and <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-hurricane-isaias-broke-through-to-become-the-first-atlantic-hurricane-in-an-extremely-quiet-2026-season-294028">upended hurricane patterns</a> – just to name a few examples.</p>

<p>But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. </p>

<p>To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-super-el-nino-why-its-too-early-to-forecast-one-with-certainty-but-not-too-soon-to-prepare-282574">has been forecasting</a> a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its <a href="https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso_advisory/ensodisc.shtml">October update</a> put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. </p>

<p>That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.</p>

<p>But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/">stopped updating</a> in May 2025. The Trump administration has also <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/27/trump-cuts-el-nino-noaa">cut or undercut</a> federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/science/science-news/meteorologists-say-nws-cuts-degraded-forecasts-recent-storms-rcna202386">daily forecasting</a>, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.  </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=TaHEoR4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">scholar of business operations and sustainability</a>, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.</p>

<h2>Gaps in climate science grow</h2>

<p>In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/nclimate2100">severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts</a>. The <a href="https://theconversation.com/as-cities-prepare-for-2026s-super-el-nino-some-crucial-blind-spots-cant-be-ignored-290787">economic hit</a> can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf2983">historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars</a>.</p>

<p>This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/time-series-US-1980-2024.csv">U.S. averaged fewer than</a> five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/beyond-data/2024-active-year-us-billion-dollar-weather-and-climate-disasters">the 2023 and 2024 totals</a> were the highest on record. </p>

<p>While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing.
That includes <a href="https://theconversation.com/extreme-weathers-true-damage-cost-is-a-mystery-thats-a-problem-for-understanding-storm-risk-257105">NOAA’s decision to retire</a> its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. </p>

<p>For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/noaa-ending-billion-dollar-disasters-database">relied on it</a> to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2025GL119127">put odds on future losses</a> or to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jue.2020.103257">forecast economic activity</a>. Some of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4013">my own research</a> also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.</p>

<p>Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. </p>

<p>In 2025 the federal government <a href="https://abcnews.com/US/trump-administration-shutters-major-federal-climate-website/story?id=123389318">shut down</a> Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2025/07/02/climate/national-climate-assessment-websites">taken offline</a>, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as <a href="https://www.weather.gov/media/notification/pdf_2025/pns25-18_Reduction_RAOB_Launches_ABR_GJT_GRB_APX_LBF_RIW.pdf">it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites</a>, which feed forecast models.</p>

<p>Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog <a href="https://www.climate.us/news-features/blogs/enso">have moved to a nonprofit</a>, while <a href="https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters">another nonprofit</a> is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Five rice farmers work in a a paddy field on the outskirts of Mumbai, India, where a late rainy season delayed the sowing of crops." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=372&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/773897/original/file-20261124-76-7wkagj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=468&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What this means for supply chains</h2>

<p>The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/science/climate-change/climate-change-data-costliest-6-months-weather-disasters-noaa-rcna238752">high administrative costs</a> and <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF12944">potential errors</a> in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. </p>

<p>In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-09/Forecast-Driven%20Supply%20Chains_%20Using%20Weather%20Data%20to%20Advance%20Logistics%20-%209.29.26%20508.pdf">data is used in supply chains</a> for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, <a href="https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2026/06/24/everyday-resilience">Walmart invests</a> heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. </p>

<p>Another example is insurance companies, which <a href="https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250520570068/en/AM-Best-Comments-on-Decommissioning-of-NOAAs-Billion-Dollar-Climate-Disaster-Database">use weather data</a> for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane <a href="https://www.tdi.texas.gov/submissions/rate_submissions/documents/rmsasop.pdf">datasets to inform</a> its advanced risk models. </p>

<p>When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/private-companies-step-up-to-gather-weather-data-for-noaa-as-staffing-cuts-hobble-agency-forecasting/">offer private weather balloon data</a> and advanced climate prediction services. </p>

<p>While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. </p>

<p>And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.</p>

<h2>What it means for consumers</h2>

<p>Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. <a href="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/APU0000713111">orange juice prices</a> to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. </p>

<p>Holiday staples are also not spared. <a href="https://abc17news.com/news/2021/12/06/christmas-trees-burned-by-the-heat-dwindling-the-supply/">A 2021 heat dome</a> in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise <a href="https://marketplace.org/2021/11/23/christmas-tree-supplies-are-tight-and-climate-change-is-to-blame">an additional 5% to 10% that year</a>. </p>

<p>And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/roses-are-red-violets-are-blue-if-cocoa-is-cheaper-why-isnt-chocolate-too">up 14% in 2026</a>. </p>

<p>A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295737/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Prepaid electricity can make bills more predictable, but not necessarily more affordable</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/773326/original/file-20261120-62-6rnieq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6058%2C4038&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Electricity isn&#39;t cheap, and consumers are feeling it.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/electricity-emitting-from-dollar-bills-held-by-a-royalty-free-image/2158443315">Photo illustration by photoschmidt/iStock/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it. If the tank ran out, there was no heat in the home, and we had to pay extra for an emergency refill and for someone to relight the pilot. A full tank of oil could last up to a month and a half – but only if we kept the heat at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) when we were home and cut it off when we went to work. </p>

<p>Where I live now, in Pennsylvania, we use natural gas and pay afterward, based on our use. It amounts to $200 to $400 monthly – and lets us keep our heat around 70 F (21 C).</p>

<p>Prepaying for heat in Massachusetts certainly made me more aware of how much heating a home cost, but it didn’t make energy cheaper or help me live according to modern standards. Instead, I got used to wearing my winter coat indoors. This is still a concern for many: As winter 2026 approached, some families in Maine that have oil heat <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/24/economy/heating-costs-struggle-maine-families">had their kids sleep in snowsuits</a> to use less fuel and keep costs down.</p>

<p>Most electricity companies bill for energy already used – like the natural gas company I have in Pennsylvania. But in Maryland, Baltimore Gas and Electric is <a href="https://dailyenergyinsider.com/news/52927-baltimore-gas-and-electric-files-new-rate-case-with-maryland-commission/">proposing a prepaid electricity program</a>, similar to my Massachusetts oil setup.</p>

<p>As an <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=PSZN_hMAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">energy affordability researcher</a> studying how <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2026.104763">people change their habits to use less energy when it’s expensive</a>, the real question for me is what this type of payment system would mean for customers. Helping households manage electricity bills is different from ensuring they can afford to <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-78-degrees-isnt-the-right-thermostat-setting-for-everyone-during-a-heat-wave-287917">use enough energy</a> at home to keep themselves safe.</p>

<h2>The company’s plan</h2>

<p>BGE, which serves approximately 1.3 million electric customers, asked Maryland Public Service Commission members to approve a <a href="https://marylandmatters.org/2026/11/19/bge-flexpay-rate-case/">prepaid program</a> for customers in July 2026. The company says this would help people keep a <a href="https://www.afro.com/sponsored/bge-highlights-its-proposed-bge-flexpay-program-as-part-of-broader-affordability-efforts-914b7818">better handle on their energy spending</a>. </p>

<p>Rather than getting a monthly bill, customers who opted into the plan would make an <a href="https://energyandpolicy.org/bge-flexpay-program-proposal/">initial $40 payment toward future electricity use</a>. They could then monitor their power usage and get alerts when balances run low.</p>

<p>The utility’s vice president of regulatory policy and strategy, John Frain, told the Maryland Public Service Commission that <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sLCsOiRqaNs&amp;t=24412s">prepaid customers wouldn’t have to pay security deposits</a> to open new accounts and wouldn’t have to worry about late payment or reconnection fees if service were disconnected because they weren’t able to pay their bills.</p>

<p>For customers with unpaid balances of up to $1,000, the company would have <a href="https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2026-11-13/maryland-consumer-advocates-worry-disconnection-rates-will-surge-under-bges-proposed-flexpay">25% of each prepayment applied to previous debts</a> and 75% go toward future electricity costs. The company expects to <a href="https://opc.maryland.gov/Portals/0/Files/Publications/Others/20260922%20-%20Defever%20Direct%20Testimony%20-%20CN%209888%20-%20Public%20Version.pdf?ver=lfuCdgu8xkVXX4y7NhPo2g==#page=125">save a yet-undetermined amount of money</a> on collection efforts.</p>

<h2>Concerns about power cuts</h2>

<p>Consumer advocates warn that <a href="https://www.originalpower.org.au/the_right_to_power">prepaid billing</a> could cause <a href="https://www.nclc.org/resources/prepaid-electric-utility-service-assessment-of-risks-and-benefits-to-low-income-consumers-in-district-of-columbia/">problems for customers</a> while making life easier for the utility company. </p>

<p>For instance, people on fixed incomes, such as Social Security, could experience <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/us/oklahoma-extreme-heat-electricity-crisis.html">increased mental stress</a> because of frequent fears their <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/2022/oct/25/why-rising-use-of-prepayment-meters-could-be-disconnection-by-back-door">electricity might be cut off</a>. </p>

<p>They also might make significant changes in their lifestyles: A 2014 study in New Zealand found customers who prepaid for their electricity <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scs.2013.10.004">rationed their own power</a> by, for instance, turning on an electric water heater only every third day and taking cold showers on other days.</p>

<p>Because Maryland prepaid customers would pay the same electricity rates as everyone else, any bill savings would likely come from living without many of the <a href="https://theconversation.com/just-because-the-bill-is-low-doesnt-mean-energy-is-affordable-289458">basic services electricity brings to modern life</a>.</p>

<p>The company’s response to this concern is that while customers whose balance gets to zero will be disconnected – as soon as the next day – they’ll have an <a href="https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2026-11-13/maryland-consumer-advocates-worry-disconnection-rates-will-surge-under-bges-proposed-flexpay">easier time getting reconnected</a>. Once people add $15 to their account, power can be restored <a href="https://www.wypr.org/wypr-news/2026-11-13/maryland-consumer-advocates-worry-disconnection-rates-will-surge-under-bges-proposed-flexpay">in less than 30 minutes</a>.</p>

<p>But even <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2026.117513">short disconnections</a> can cause big problems. For people dependent on <a href="https://stories.usatodaynetwork.com/hostagetoheat/prepaid-utility-plans-leave-some-customers-without-electricity">electric-powered medical devices, such as breathing equipment</a> or <a href="https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/professionals/diabetes-discoveries-practice/disaster-planning-for-patients-with-kidney-disease">home dialysis machines</a>, getting disconnected can injure or kill them. Without the power to charge a phone or power a Wi-Fi router, some people <a href="https://embed.documentcloud.org/documents/28677894/annotations/2832499/?embed=1">may have trouble getting alerts about their balance</a> or making payments to turn their electricity back on. </p>

<h2>Keeping the lights on, even in hardship</h2>

<p>Under <a href="https://regs.maryland.gov/us/md/exec/comar/20.31.02.05">traditional billing, Maryland law</a> gives customers protections against rapid disconnections. When people are late paying their bills, utilities have to notify them of the overdue balance and give them at least 14 days to pay before cutting off power – a period during which they can still use electricity.</p>

<p>This delay gives people a chance to make <a href="https://www.bge.com/my-account/my-dashboard/pay-my-bill/payment-arrangements">payment arrangements</a> and <a href="https://opc.maryland.gov/Portals/0/Files/Publications/Consumer-Learning/Consumer%20Rights%20Packet%20FY26%20English.pdf">seek financial assistance</a>, such as from the state’s <a href="https://dhs.maryland.gov/office-of-home-energy-programs/about-energy-assistance/">Office of Home Energy Programs</a>. </p>

<p>Applying to that office allows customers to request an additional <a href="https://dhs.maryland.gov/office-of-home-energy-programs/frequently-asked-questions/">55-day reprieve from disconnection</a>, which can <a href="https://theconversation.com/america-faces-a-power-disconnection-crisis-amid-dangerous-heat-in-27-states-utilities-can-shut-off-electricity-for-nonpayment-even-in-a-heat-wave-234865">help families stay connected</a> during extreme weather events.</p>

<h2>Pilot programs</h2>

<p>In August 2019, BGE conducted a trial run of the prepaid system with 527 customers.</p>

<p>An independent analysis found that power disconnections were often shorter – <a href="https://www.appriseinc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Final-BGE-Prepaid-Pilot-Evaluation-Report.pdf">five hours on average</a> – for prepaid customers than for customers who were billed later for the power they used, whose power was off for an average of 9.4 days. But 10% of prepaid customers had their power cut off at some point during the test period, compared with just 1% of those in the traditional billing program.</p>

<p>The trial run generated some positive outcomes for customers: <a href="https://www.appriseinc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Final-BGE-Prepaid-Pilot-Evaluation-Report.pdf">61% of the participants said they had better control</a> over their energy bills by being able to decide when and how much to prepay, and 34% said the program’s feature of progressively paying off overdue bills helped them.</p>

<p>However, 41% of participants left before the program formally ended in November 2020. <a href="https://www.appriseinc.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Final-BGE-Prepaid-Pilot-Evaluation-Report.pdf#page=39">Among those who left</a>, one-third didn’t like making frequent payments, and 23% felt their energy cost more.</p>

              <span class="caption">If the price of power is the same, the payment method doesn’t improve affordability, even if it can help consumers monitor costs.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/UtilityPrices/1b17889e638043fcbfd862e6daa81167/photo">AP Photo/Jenny Kane</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>A way to help consumers without also hurting them?</h2>

<p>BGE told Maryland officials that the prepaid program is “<a href="https://opc.maryland.gov/Portals/0/Files/Publications/Others/20260922%20-%20Howat%20Direct%20-%20CN%209888.pdf?ver=USvpQDkpPuBrT7mg8DIVRw==#page=66">not intended as a cost-savings program for customers</a>.” </p>

<p>The company says its prepay program offers customers online tools to monitor their energy use and the option to make payments when it’s financially convenient.</p>

<p>But BGE customers can <a href="https://www.bge.com/my-account/my-dashboard/pay-my-bill">already do both of those things online</a>. </p>

<p>And a utility that cuts people off for running out of credit <a href="https://www.nclc.org/states-can-bring-down-unaffordable-utility-bills/">has less incentive to help customers actually afford sufficient levels</a> of energy to live their lives. That’s because investor-owned utilities generally don’t earn money on selling more electricity, but rather <a href="https://opc.maryland.gov/Consumer-Learning/Utility-Rates-and-Basics">on building and maintaining power lines and substations</a>. In fact, if systemwide energy use drops – due to mild weather or people <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2024.103528">choosing to use less energy</a> – and the utility collects less than its approved revenue target, then Maryland law lets it <a href="https://materials.proxyvote.com/Approved/30161N/20260302/FO10K_626616/INDEX.HTML?page=176">charge customers more</a> so the utility can <a href="https://affordability-toolkit.rmi.org/policies/revenue-decoupling">cover its costs and still make a profit</a>.</p>

<p>The Maryland Public Service Commission will decide on BGE’s proposal in January 2027. Its ruling on this prepaid electricity system will determine whether people who seek greater control over their monthly bills would have to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2024.103666">give up legal protections</a> that help customers continue to meet their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.enpol.2023.113813">basic energy needs</a> without sacrificing their health and safety during <a href="https://theconversation.com/new-federal-figures-reveal-1-in-3-us-households-struggle-to-pay-energy-bills-but-the-reality-is-likely-even-worse-279627">financial hardships</a>.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296551/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772254/original/file-20261116-64-zhdurv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5862%2C3908&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">About half a million Californians were affected by the state&#39;s hike in minimum wage for fast-food workers.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/California%20Fast%20Food%20Wages/e927c74290594149bb3b0c07b60c42b0/photo">AP Photo/Jae C. Hong</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been <a href="https://www.epi.org/minimum-wage-tracker/?gad_source=1&amp;gad_campaignid=887095437&amp;gbraid=0AAAAADncI6rj-2kyPIUANBmaG-1Vug3Ah&amp;gclid=Cj0KCQiAworYBhDoARIsAP5ft3Jkjs1ngB9lOT3zh1LRFL6tQ5xsQpJ17Bgd3976iRs-4quajZzjQvIaAge0EALw_wcB">raising their minimum wage</a> on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries. </p>

<p>As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results.</p>

<p>In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that <a href="https://www.gov.ca.gov/2023/09/28/california-increases-minimum-wage-protections-for-fast-food-workers/">more than 500,000 workers would be covered</a> by this mandate.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=pw4MddIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">researcher of health and labor markets</a>, I joined with economists <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Jh-oGMwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">David Neumark</a>, <a href="https://louisiana.edu/directory/people/gary-wagner">Gary Wagner</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=pw4MddIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Vitor Melo</a> to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3386/w35749">run a study</a> measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs. </p>

<p>We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at.</p>

<p>For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%.</p>

<p>This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain.</p>

<p>The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of <a href="https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/wages/minimumwage">$7.25 an hour</a> has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own.</p>

<p><a href="https://hrwatchdog.calchamber.com/2026/06/los-angeles-city-revises-wage-and-health-benefits-requirements-for-hotel-airport-workers/">Los Angeles is phasing in</a> a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received <a href="https://www.cmadocs.org/newsroom/news/view/ArticleId/51201/Health-care-worker-minimum-wage-increases-under-SB-525-take-effect-July-1">another scheduled increase</a>. Vermont lawmakers <a href="https://vtdigger.org/2026/02/04/fast-food-wage-bill-would-raise-minimum-pay-to-20-an-hour-in-2027/">have proposed</a> a $20 fast-food wage of their own.</p>

<p>In addition, a total of 16 states will <a href="https://www.epi.org/blog/sixteen-states-will-raise-their-minimum-wages-on-january-1-lifting-pay-for-over-6-6-million-workers/">raise their minimum wages</a> across the board on Jan. 1, 2027. </p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Smaller chains see an impact</h2>

<p>The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists. </p>

<p>In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage <a href="https://doi.org/10.3386/w34033">caused small declines</a> in employment compared with other states; <a href="https://irle.berkeley.edu/publications/working-papers/effects-of-a-20-minimum-wage-evidence-from-granular-data-on-wages-employment-and-prices/">others contend</a> that the effect on jobs is essentially zero. </p>

<p>More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger <a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/long-run-employment-effects-minimum-wage-putty-clay-perspective">in the long run</a>. </p>

<p>Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage?</p>

<p>We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures. </p>

<p>We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones.</p>

<p>For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period.</p>

<p>But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose.</p>

<p>How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones.</p>

<p>A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses.</p>

<h2>Taking the longer view</h2>

<p>First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although <a href="https://doi.org/10.3386/w34990">other research suggests</a> they rose by 3% to 4%. </p>

<p>That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains.</p>

<p>Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that <a href="https://cepr.org/voxeu/columns/reallocation-effects-minimum-wage">other researchers</a> documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage.</p>

<p>For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294552/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Why the Army wants to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa
excerpt: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Im
body: A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Images This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

In Iowa, the Pentagon is preparing to send a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving — by blowing up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive, in order to dispose of it.  The detonation was briefly halted by a lower court before a federal circuit court cleared the way on Monday, and it now appears set to take place on Wednesday morning.  According to the Army , there’s a real need for haste: The lead azide is sufficiently unstable that it’s at risk of detonating on its own in an uncontrolled explosion, and falling temperatures in Iowa reportedly make such an explosion more likely
An uncontrolled explosion would also be more dangerous and unpredictable, and potentially cause worse lead pollution

At the same time, though, Iowa residents are angry and alarmed by a lack of clear information, poor communication by the Army, and the potential health hazards.  The potential for things to go sideways has President Donald Trump nervous enough that he tried to pass the decision to Rob Sand — not the current Iowa governor, but the incoming Democratic governor- elect — and let any consequences fall on his head
But as of Tuesday, it appears the detonation will go forward with court approval

The lead plume produced by the blast — which will take place inside reinforced concrete bunkers, along with other steps to mitigate the risk — could still spread as far as 100 miles from the site, according to the Washington Post .  The American Lung Association has urged anyone near the blast to remain inside for one to two days afterward, among other guidance, and on Tuesday, the Health & Human Services Department recommended that children and pregnant women evacuate from the path of the plume, which could stretch into neighboring Missouri

The lead risk all around us Emergency munitions detonations in the US are pretty rare — there are, thankfully, better ways to dispose of toxic materials these days (and questions about why the Army didn’t pursue them in this case).  But despite a great deal of progress in the US — including banning things like new lead paint and pipes and leaded gasoline in the 20th century — lead remains a serious public health threat.  Part of that is because of how dangerous it really is: Lead is not just a neurotoxin, but one with no safe levels of human exposure; even a little bit can be harmful, especially to children.  But as my colleague Dylan Scott  reported in 2024, it also keeps popping up nearly everywhere we look, including in our food supply.  According to Dylan’s reporting , there are three big reasons for lead’s seeming inescapability: Active disregard, negligence, and the fact that it’s just really hard to get rid of

Lead was widely used in the US decades ago, before those bans on lead paint and leaded gasoline, and some of that lead is still around, in the soil, in old houses, and in other materials dating back to that time

It’s also not a problem that the US can easily address alone, since lots of lead exposure is the result of goods being imported into the US.  “If we really want to solve this,” Drew McCartor, the director of a global public health nonprofit, told Dylan at the time, “it requires a whole-­of-­government commitment to work outside of our borders.” One link for later ➨ Follow “Maslow’s hierarchy of hosting.” Thanksgiving is almost upon us, and if you’re feeling a little angsty about your holiday obligations, consider this guidance from the event planner Megan Fitzgerald: Your hosting needs, at a minimum, start with a clean space, a bathroom stocked with adequate toilet paper, and enough cups and water to go around. (Plus, of course, the food.) Basically, everything else is extra

Before you go… Did you know… that, with very few exceptions, US grocery stores sell only one breed of turkey ? It’s called the Broad Breasted White turkey, and it’s been bred to grow twice as fast (and become nearly twice as big) as its forebears did in the 1960s

You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword

Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked you which 19th-century author and activist is known as “the mother of Black feminism.” That would be Anna Julia Cooper, who was one of the first African American women to receive a PhD
She lived to 105, well into the 20th century.

title: How Donald Trump warped the most important law protecting assault victims on campus
excerpt: Protesters at a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe on October 13, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Imag
body: Protesters at a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe on October 13, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images In the weeks since reports about an alleged gang rape at Cornell University went public, I’ve heard a lot of people ask why we haven’t made more progress on campus sexual assault
I started working on the issue as a student activist more than 15 years ago
Now, as an attorney at Public Justice, I represent student survivors of sexual assault in lawsuits against their schools
Seeing the stories out of Cornell sometimes makes me feel like nothing has changed since I was an undergraduate
But that’s not quite right: We did make progress

Schools started taking more seriously their responsibilities to address sexual assaults, providing survivors with academic and mental health support to help them stay in school and setting up procedures to investigate allegations
This progress was spurred significantly by enforcement of Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex discrimination in education and offers protections to student survivors of sexual assault
However, that progress was met by backlash — both political backlash specific to Title IX and a broader hostility to civil rights in the federal courts
As a result, Title IX is now less effective in protecting student survivors than it was a decade ago
And in some ways, Title IX now effectively encourages schools to mistreat victims
What a bitter irony for a sex discrimination law
Some of these changes, such as the Trump administration’s rewriting of Title IX’s regulations, have received plenty of public attention

But others have flown under the radar, including a 2022 Supreme Court decision that reduced the damages available in Title IX lawsuits, as well as the rise of “reverse discrimination” lawsuits by men accused of sexual harassment
Despite the lack of attention, their effects on students have been significant
But this doesn’t mean we have to resign ourselves to a steady unwinding of progress
There are other routes survivors can take to hold schools accountable for tolerating sexual violence on campus
Trump twisted Title IX around Since President Richard Nixon signed Title IX into law in 1972, federal agencies have enforced the sex discrimination law against schools

Title IX is perhaps best known for ushering in a revolution in women’s sports, but addresses a wide range of forms of sex discrimination, including pregnancy discrimination, sex-segregated classrooms, and sexual harassment
Starting in the 1990s, the Education Department began publishing guidance documents that outlined schools’ Title IX responsibilities to address sexual harassment, including sexual assault

These covered topics like definitions of sexual harassment and how schools are supposed to respond to reports, mostly leaving the minutiae of schools’ investigatory and disciplinary procedures to their own discretion

Under President Barack Obama, the US Department of Education issued a number of high-profile guidances and ramped up enforcement efforts, with the goal of pushing schools to respect victims’ Title IX rights, which many had long ignored
Those developments were lauded by student activists and civil rights groups
But critics on the right, and some on the left, saw these changes as going too far to protect survivors at the cost of due process of the accused
In 2020, the first Trump administration put its own, very different, stamp on Title IX
It promulgated a new set of Title IX regulations that govern how the Department of Education analyzes administrative complaints it receives through its Office for Civil Rights
President Joe Biden tried to replace these regulations in 2024, but two courts struck them down early the next year
So Trump’s 2020 regulations are back in effect today

The 2020 regulations are most known for the procedural requirements they require of schools investigating sexual harassment — requirements that are often understood to protect accused students, though they are so complicated that they might chiefly benefit whoever can afford to pay an attorney.  At colleges and universities, the regulations require schools to use a single onerous and adversarial hearing model in which the parties’ representatives directly cross-examine the witnesses, including the survivor
Some students choose a lawyer as their representative, but some pick a parent or friend
As a result, at Cornell, Jane Doe could have been directly cross-examined by one of the accused men’s dads or fraternity brothers
Understandably, this process can be retraumatizing for survivors
Some refuse to pursue an investigation as a result.  That’s a real shame, because there are other truth-seeking options that schools use in other kinds of disciplinary matters

In imposing this one-size-fits-all model, the rules forbid schools from using hearing models that courts have blessed as constitutional, and which reduce face-to-face conflict by routing the parties’ questions through neutral third parties
There is more to the 2020 regulations than process, though
Less reported are the changes they made to Title IX’s liability standard — that is, what kinds of harassment schools have to address and how good of a job schools are expected to do

Under previous administrations, Democratic and Republican alike, the Department of Education interpreted Title IX to require schools to respond to severe or pervasive harassment, and to do so promptly and effectively

The Trump regulations instead require schools only to address severe and pervasive harassment, and to respond in a way that is not “deliberately indifferent” or “clearly unreasonable.”  That means that schools are allowed, under current regulations, to ignore reported sexual harassment until it escalates and to then treat the victim unreasonably — so long as that response isn’t clearly unreasonable

In practice, that might mean that the Department of Education will tolerate a school dragging its feet to investigate, or failing to provide a survivor the academic accommodations she needs after a sexual assault, so long as the Department believes those failures were merely unreasonable and not “clearly” so.   Trump justified the 2020 regulations as necessary to protect the accused, but the most significant provisions instead protect schools like Cornell from liability for mistreating survivors

Schools have less reason to fear Title IX complaints filed against them by victims with the Department of Education because, when it comes to doing right by survivors, the federal government expects less of schools now.  The Supreme Court also changed the landscape       In addition to reporting to the Department of Education, students can also file Title IX lawsuits against their schools in court

Van Hollen, who previously served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2016, said the party needs a fresh face to deliver the change voters demanded when they handed Dems such big victories in the midterms.  In an interview on Vox’s America, Actually podcast, Van Hollen told host Astead Herndon that Schumer has been too timid in confronting Trump and the Republican Party, and too unwilling to use unconventional means to try to rally support for Democratic causes. “My view is that working outside the Congress to highlight the attacks on our democracy was essential

You can’t just use the same tools that were used before Trump to take on a lawless Trump,” Van Hollen said. “We need to organize in this moment to help protect our democracy and our Constitution and get things done and deliver.” Herndon spoke with Van Hollen ahead of the December 1 vote that will decide the chamber’s Democratic leadership for the new Congress; below is an excerpt of their, edited for length and clarity.  There’s much more in the full show, including how Van Hollen would handle the looming government funding deadline and a possible shutdown over the Iran war; his approach to reining in funding for Israel and finding a path forward to improve the US healthcare system; and his plans for holding the Trump administration accountable.  You can listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel

President, we’re not going to give you this blank check in order to carry out these attacks on our Constitution, to see these ICE raids where they were undermining constitutional rights, killing American citizens in the streets of Minneapolis.”  All of that needed to be resisted early on
I helped organize the first protest demonstration against Elon Musk taking his chainsaw to USAID
We also went to highlight that lawlessness in front of other federal agencies
My view is that working outside the Congress to highlight the attacks on our democracy was essential
You can’t just use the same tools that were used before Trump to take on a lawless Trump
It sounds like you’re talking about making the position more of an activist organizer position and leading from the front more than we saw Schumer do over the last couple years

Elissa Slotkin of Michigan supported me, which shows that this is not a progressive versus moderate thing
It really is a question of taking on an economy rigged for the wealthy against working people
