title: Millions of turkeys will be thrown in the trash this Thanksgiving
excerpt: A turkey arrives at the 2024 White House turkey pardon, a strange annual “song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them,” as Vox’s Kenny Torrella
body: A turkey arrives at the 2024 White House turkey pardon, a strange annual “song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them,” as Vox’s Kenny Torrella put it last year. | Susan Walsh/Associated Press This week, tens of millions of Americans will partake in a national ritual many of us say we don’t especially enjoy or find meaning in

We will collectively eat tens of millions of turkeys , factory-farmed and heavily engineered animals that bear scant resemblance to the wild birds that have been apocryphally written into the Thanksgiving story. (The first Thanksgiving probably didn’t have turkey.) And we will do it all even though turkey meat is widely considered flavorless and unpalatable.  “It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout,” journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice . “Deep down, we know this, but bury it beneath happy memories of Thanksgivings past.”  So what is essentially the national holiday of meat-eating revolves around an animal dish that no one really likes

That fact clashes with the widely accepted answer to the central question of why it’s so hard to convince everyone to ditch meat , or even to eat less of it: the taste, stupid.   Undoubtedly, that has something to do with it

But I think the real answer is a lot more complicated, and the tasteless Thanksgiving turkey explains why.  Inside this story Why Americans eat turkey on Thanksgiving, despite many of us not liking it very much! What life is like for a Thanksgiving turkey
What to eat instead of turkey, and why you might even see going turkey-free as more authentic to the values of Thanksgiving
Humans crave ritual, belonging, and a sense of being part of a larger story — aspirations that reach their apotheosis at the Thanksgiving table

We don’t want to be social deviants who boycott the central symbol of one of our most cherished national holidays, reminding everyone of the animal torture and environmental degradation that went into making it

What could be more human than to go along with it, dry meat and all?  Our instincts for conformity seem particularly strong around food, a social glue that binds us to one another and to our shared past

And although many of us today recognize there’s something very wrong with how our meat is produced , Thanksgiving of all occasions might seem like an ideal time to forget that for a day.  In my experience, plenty of people who are trying to cut back on meat say they eat vegetarian or vegan when cooking for themselves — but when they are guests at other people’s homes or celebrating a special occasion, they’ll eat whatever, to avoid offending their hosts or provoking awkward conversations about factory farming.  But this Thanksgiving, I want to invite you to flip this logic

If the social and cultural context of food shapes our tastes, even more than taste itself, then it is in precisely these settings that we should focus efforts to change American food customs for the better.  “It’s eating with others where we actually have an opportunity to influence broader change, to share plant-based recipes, spark discussion, and revamp traditions to make them more sustainable and compassionate,” Natalie Levin, an acquaintance of mine from vegan Twitter, told me a few years ago
Hundreds of years ago, a turkey on Thanksgiving might have represented abundance and good tidings — a too-rare thing in those days, and therefore something to be grateful for
Today, it’s hard to see it as anything but a symbol of our profligacy and unrestrained cruelty against nonhuman animals
On a day meant to embody the best of humanity, and a vision for a more perfect world, surely we can come up with better symbols.  Besides, we don’t even like turkey
We should skip it this year.  The misery of the Thanksgiving turkey  In 2023, my colleague Kenny Torrella published a wrenching investigation into conditions in the US turkey industry

He wrote:  The Broad Breasted White turkey, which accounts for 99 out of every 100 grocery store turkeys , has been bred to emphasize — you guessed it — the breast, one of the more valuable parts of the bird
These birds grow twice as fast and become nearly twice as big as they did in the 1960s
Being so top-heavy, combined with other health issues caused by rapid growth and the unsanitary factory farming environment, can make it difficult for them to walk
Another problem arises from their giant breasts: The males get so big that they can’t mount the hens, so they must be bred artificially
Author Jim Mason detailed this practice in his book The Ethics of What We Eat , co-authored with philosopher Peter Singer

Mason took a job with the turkey giant Butterball to research the book, where, he wrote , he had to hold male turkeys while another worker stimulated them to extract their semen into a syringe using a vacuum pump
Once the syringe was full, it was taken to the henhouse, where Mason would pin hens chest-down while another worker inserted the contents of the syringe into the hen using an air compressor
Workers at the farm had to do this to one hen every 12 seconds for 10 hours a day
It was “the hardest, fastest, dirtiest, most disgusting, worst-paid work” he had ever done, Mason wrote

In the wild, turkeys live in “smallish groups of a dozen or so, and they know each other, they relate to each other as individuals,” Singer, author of the book Consider the Turkey , said on an episode of the Simple Heart podcast. “The turkeys sold on Thanksgiving never see their mothers, they never go and forage for food…They’re pretty traumatized, I’d say, by having thousands of strange birds around who they can’t get to know as individuals,” packed together in crowded sheds.  From birth to death, the life of a factory-farmed turkey is one punctuated by rote violence, including mutilations to their beaks, their toes, and snoods , a grueling trip to the slaughterhouse, and a killing process where they’re roughly grabbed and prodded, shackled upside down, and sent down a fast-moving conveyor belt of killing. “If they’re lucky, they get stunned and then the knife cuts their throat,” Singer said. “If they’re not so lucky, they miss the stunner and the knife cuts their throat while they’re fully conscious.”  A 2024 estimate by ReFED , a nonprofit that works to reduce food waste, found that Americans throw the equivalent of more than 8 million of these turkeys in the trash

And this year will be the fifth Thanksgiving in a row celebrated amid an out-of-control bird flu outbreak , in which tens of millions of chickens and turkeys on infected farms have been culled using stomach-churning extermination methods .  Reclaiming Thanksgiving When I search for the language for this grim state of affairs, I can only describe it in religious terms, as a kind of desecration — of our planet’s abundance, of our humanity, of life itself
On every other day of the year, it’s obscene enough

On a holiday that’s supposed to represent our gratitude for the Earth’s blessings, you can understand why Thanksgiving is often described by vegans and vegetarians as the most alienating day of the year.  I count myself among that group, although I don’t dread Thanksgiving
I’ve come to love it as an opportune time for creative reinvention

I usually spend it making a feast of plant-based dishes (known by most people as “sides,” though there’s no reason they can’t be the main event).  To name a few: a mushroom Wellington , a creamy lentil-stuffed squash , cashew lentil bake , a bright autumnal Brussels sprout salad , roasted red cabbage with walnuts and feta (sub with dairy-free cheese ), mushroom clam-less chowder (I add lots of white beans), challah for bread rolls, a pumpkin miso tart more complex and interesting than any Thanksgiving pie you’ve had, and rasmalai , a Bengali dessert whose flavors align beautifully with the holidays. This year I’m making this legitimately mind-blowing tiramisu, which can be made ridiculously easy by substituting Biscoff cookies (or similar) for the ladyfingers
Vegan turkey roasts are totally optional, though many of them have gotten very good in recent years — I love the Gardein breaded roast and Field Roast hazelnut and cranberry

You can also make your own .    The hardest part of going meatless is not about the food (if it were, it might not be so hard to convince Americans to abandon parched roast turkey). “It’s about unpleasant truths and ethical disagreements being brought out into the open,” Levin said, about confronting the bizarre dissonance in celebrations of joy and giving carved from mass-produced violence.  These conversations are not easy, but they are worth having
And we don’t have to fear losing the rituals that define us as Americans
To the contrary, culture is a continuous conversation we have with each other about what we hold dear — and any culture that’s not changing is dead
There’s more meaning to be had in adapting traditions that are no longer authentic to our values
Update, November 24, 2026, 11:55 am ET: This story was originally published in 2024 and has been updated for 202 6.

title: The Supreme Court is about to decide if assault rifle bans can exist
excerpt: Activists rally outside the Supreme Court before a Second Amendment case in 2023. | Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images On December 2, the Supreme Cou
body: Activists rally outside the Supreme Court before a Second Amendment case in 2023. | Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images On December 2, the Supreme Court will hear two cases asking whether lawmakers may ban so-called assault rifles, semiautomatic weapons equipped with various features that allow a shooter to fire many rounds with greater accuracy than if they used an ordinary rifle

The cases involve two similar laws, one out of Cook County, Illinois and another out of Connecticut, that seek to ban civilian ownership of AR-15s, a popular gun that was used in several recent mass shootings, and similar weapons

While there are subtle differences between the two laws, both ban semiautomatic rifles with features such as pistol grips that reduce recoil and make it easier for a shooter to rapidly fire many shots at a target. (There is a chance that the Cook County case will be declared moot , but if that happens the Court will still be able to decide the Connecticut case.) The most striking thing about the briefs in these two cases, Viramontes v
Higgins , is that they describe two entirely different Second Amendments that operate in completely different ways
Yet both of these competing Second Amendments can be found in this Court’s precedents

It’s unclear just how much the Court’s decision to choose one Second Amendment over the other will matter to future cases, because the Court sometimes reaches results in gun rights cases that are difficult to justify under any of its previous precedents — the most consistent pattern in this Court’s Second Amendment decisions is that both Democratic and Republican justices typically reach the result that is preferred by their political party
But, at the very least, Viramontes and Grant give the justices an opportunity to bring coherence to one of the most disordered areas in US constitutional law
The lawyers defending the assault rifle bans rely heavily on the Court’s decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v

Bruen (2022), a chaotic decision which held that all gun laws are unconstitutional unless the government can show that they fit within “this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.” Though Bruen is often criticized by the Court’s Democratic minority, the lawyers on the anti-assault rifle side of Viramontes and Grant argue that, for seven centuries, both English and American lawmakers have enacted laws that target weapons they deem “ unusually dangerous ,” and thus a ban on assault rifles fits well within this historical tradition
The pro-gun side’s brief , meanwhile, engages with these historical arguments only as an afterthought
Instead, they primarily rely on a political compromise between Justice Antonin Scalia, the author of the Supreme Court’s landmark Second Amendment decision in District of Columbia v
Heller (2008), and Justice Anthony Kennedy, a more moderate conservative

According to the late Justice John Paul Stevens, Kennedy agreed to join Scalia’s opinion in Heller , but only if Scalia agreed to add some language limiting Heller ’s impact and ensuring that many gun regulations would survive .  Ironically, the pro-gun side in Viramontes and Grant now argue that this compromise requires the modern-day Court to legalize assault rifles in all 50 states, even as the side arguing in favor of assault rifle bans rely on the broadly pro-gun framework announced in Bruen
Realistically, it is likely that this Supreme Court, with its 6-3 Republican majority, will choose the path that the pro-gun side prefers
As that side notes in its brief , three current justices, including Justice Brett Kavanaugh, have previously suggested that assault rifle bans are unconstitutional
And the Court’s previous decisions applying Bruen often bend the rules to ensure that the pro-gun side wins
But, if the Court does somehow decide to uphold these laws, it will be because Viramontes and Grant are the rare cases where Bruen cuts in favor of the pro-gun control side

The two Second Amendments, explained The Second Amendment states that “A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed,” and up until fairly recently, the Supreme Court took the first thirteen words of this amendment very seriously

Miller (1939), the “obvious purpose” of the Second Amendment was to “render possible the effectiveness” of militias, and the amendment must be “interpreted and applied with that end in view.” The Court abandoned this textualist approach to gun rights, however, in District of Columbia v

Heller (2008), which held that the Second Amendment protects an individual right to possess a gun for personal “self-defense.” The bulk of the Heller opinion is a complicated originalist argument that, despite the amendment’s words, its actual purpose is to “guarantee the individual right to possess and carry weapons in case of confrontation.” But Heller also includes three anomalous paragraphs — Section III of the opinion — which enumerate several types of gun regulation that are not prohibited by the Second Amendment

The Court declares, for example, that laws forbidding “possession of firearms by felons and the mentally ill,” or “the carrying of firearms in sensitive places such as schools and government buildings,” or “prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons,’” are all consistent with Heller . (As I’ll get into below, this last line, the one about “dangerous and unusual” weapons, plays a starring role in the pro-gun side’s brief in Viramontes and Grant .) Shortly before his death in 2019, retired Justice Stevens revealed some of the internal deliberations that led Scalia to insert this list of exceptions to the Second Amendment

According to Stevens, then-Justice Kennedy asked Scalia to make “some important changes” to the Heller opinion after Scalia’s original draft was circulated to the full Court — and, because the non-Kennedy justices split 4-4 in Heller , Scalia had to accommodate Kennedy if he wanted to remain in the majority
And so Scalia added Section III of the Heller opinion as a political compromise to secure Kennedy’s fifth vote
This compromise could have died in 2022, when the Court handed down Bruen

Bruen , after all, held that judges should determine the meaning of the Second Amendment by asking whether a modern day law fits within a “historical tradition of firearm regulation.” Under this test, government lawyers must show that the modern-day gun law they are defending is sufficiently similar to “analogous regulations” that existed when the Constitution was framed.  That’s obviously a different legal rule than the one laid out in Section III of Heller , which turned on a private negotiation between Scalia and Kennedy

But Kennedy’s successor, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a separate concurring opinion in Bruen that explicitly endorsed the Heller compromise — Kavanaugh even blockquoted most of Section III of Heller in that concurring opinion
And Kavanaugh’s concurring opinion was joined by Chief Justice John Roberts
So the Heller compromise is still alive today because, even on a 6-3 Republican Supreme Court, two members of the majority want to keep that compromise alive
For Second Amendment litigators, this means that gun rights cases often have to proceed on two different tracks

If a gun rights plaintiff challenges a gun law that doesn’t fit within one of the Heller ’s enumerated exceptions to the Second Amendment, then judges can resolve the case by using the historical analysis demanded by Bruen (an analysis, it’s worth noting, that nearly always results in the law being struck down — at least if the case reaches the Supreme Court)
But if a gun law does fit within one of Heller ’s exceptions, Roberts and Kavanaugh may potentially form a majority with the Court’s three Democrats to uphold the law
What makes Viramontes and Grant , the assault rifle cases, unusual is that the two sides of the case have flipped on whether Bruen or Section III of Heller should apply

The side that wants legal assault rifles in every state leans hard into Heller ’s line about “dangerous and unusual weapons,” claiming that assault rifles are actually very common in the United States and therefore not “unusual” at all
At one point in their brief, they claim that “approximately 26 million people” currently own an AR-15 or similar gun

Meanwhile, the lawyers supporting assault rifle bans cite multiple historical examples of English and early American laws that banned commonly used weapons after lawmakers determined that those weapons are too dangerous to be widely available
These lawyers, in other words, essentially ask the Court to look past the Heller compromise and apply the (ordinarily very pro-gun) framework laid out in Bruen

The briefs defending the assault rifle bans are extraordinarily persuasive, and they have almost no chance of winning five votes on this Supreme Court Connecticut’s brief defending its assault rifle ban opens with a harrowing reminder of why the state passed this law — in 2012, “a lone gunman armed with an AR-15-style rifle murdered twenty first-graders and six educators inside Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut.” It’s clear that Connecticut’s leaders care a great deal about preserving this law
Among other things, they hired former US Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar — in my opinion the single best Supreme Court advocate in the country right now — as their lead counsel
Prelogar is also the only lawyer to successfully defend a gun law before the Supreme Court after Bruen was handed down
Rahimi (2024), she persuaded the Court to uphold a federal law that disarms people who are subject to domestic violence restraining orders

title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
excerpt: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "com
body: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sentience as "completely idiotic." But the belief isn't totally fringe: In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious

Form versus function: The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

Anthropic's business model could be its own trap: If the company ever concluded its AI models were truly sentient, running them around the clock in data centers—and shutting them down—would become a moral catastrophe, one the company itself flagged as an investor risk. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149569" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI
To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing

Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.  Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.  This thinking isn’t all that fringe
According to one recent poll , 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have

In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).  But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place
Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat
Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is , Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat
But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know
Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer
You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness

In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.  The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI
There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week

Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre .” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet
Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course
This is still a philosophical question for now
But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York
He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language

An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience

Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.  Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin
Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines
If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place
Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers

This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement
But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right
AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield
The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers
Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether

If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process
Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size
But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

title: Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
excerpt: Rocks have limits: New research suggests that spreading crushed rock on farmland to capture carbon — a practice called enhanced rock weathering — could raise so
body: Rocks have limits: New research suggests that spreading crushed rock on farmland to capture carbon — a practice called enhanced rock weathering — could raise soil pH to levels that harm crops, potentially capping the method's usefulness at a fraction of earlier estimates
Big money, big questions: Tech giants including Google have committed hundreds of millions to ERW, even as scientists debate whether some projects have overstated how much carbon they actually remove

The science is still catching up: Researchers say lingering questions about key variables — including how much carbon will make it to the oceans — introduce serious uncertainty about what's permanent, and what's just wishful accounting. " data-chronoton-post-id="1149392" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away

A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming
An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.  Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year
The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it , which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years. “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”   How it works There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon
Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid

When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.  The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells
As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing. “Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process
Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations
But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal
Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point)

Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.  So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone). “It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale

We know it works kinetically.” “If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.” Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture
One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%. “That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says

Agricultural limits But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels)

But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.  Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory
That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue
That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says

That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated. “All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”  The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals
Rising popularity Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW

In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering

That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.  Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.  He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean
But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector

A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts

Tempered expectations   The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “ more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann , who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies
In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method

The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.  CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans

That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post

Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades. “I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.” Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post
